When $A$ is quasi-Gorenstein, this module is identified with the first syzygy of the canonical module $ω_{A/xA}$, for any $x\in\operatorname{ann}_A K^{d-1}(A)$ that is regular on $A$. This recovers a theorem of Tavanfar and Shimomoto for quasi-Gorenstein deformations of a 3-dimensional quasi-Gorenstein local ring $A$ with $K^2(A)\cong k$. We also construct examples of section rings satisfying the hypotheses of our theorem.

items.title: Rough Stochastic Viscous Camassa-Holm equation
items.summary: In this paper, we establish well-posedness results for the viscous Camassa--Holm equation driven by the additive Gaussian noise $(1-\partial_x^2)^{-η}ξ$, where $ξ$ denotes the space-time white noise and $η>-1/12$. This formulation includes spatially colored noise for $η>0$, space-time white noise for $η=0$, and rough noise for $-1/12<η<0$. More precisely, we establish a pathwise solution theory via approximation by equations driven by regularized noises. The main difficulty arises from the singular interactions between the nonlinear terms and the irregular stochastic convolution. By introducing suitable enhanced stochastic objects and applying paracontrolled techniques, we obtain local well-posedness for the full range $η>-1/12$. Furthermore, when $η>1/4$, we establish global well-posedness by deriving suitable energy estimates.

items.title: Elastic wave propagation in fractured media with spring-type and frictional contact deformation laws
items.summary: Elastic wave propagation in fractured media is relevant to applications such as analysis of seismic waves and non-destructive characterization of materials. Understanding attenuation and scattering behavior arising from wave-fracture interaction is important for interpreting observations at both field and laboratory scales. This work presents a computational method for elastic wave propagation in fractured media based on a mixed-dimensional discrete fracture-matrix representation. Fracture deformation is governed by four models of increasing complexity, ranging from widely used spring-based formulations to frictional fracture contact models. Many previous studies are restricted to simplified wave fields, single fractures or subsets of the relevant fracture deformation mechanisms. In contrast, the proposed methodology enables fully coupled simulation of elastic wave propagation with fracture deformation models that account for elastic normal deformation, frictional contact and fracture opening and closure. The elastic wave equation is discretized in space using the cell-centered finite volume method Multi-Point Stress Approximation with weak symmetry and in time using the Newmark method. The spatial discretization is locally conservative and applicable to general polyhedral grids, making it well suited for media containing fractures, material heterogeneities and anisotropy. The proposed methodology is verified through numerical convergence analyses and is subsequently applied to wave propagation and fracture deformation in two- and three-dimensional media containing multiple intersecting fractures, demonstrating the influence of fracture constitutive behavior on wave transmission, scattering and fracture deformation.

items.title: Solutions to the Fokker-Planck equation with time-dependent force and source in $\mathbb R^3$
items.summary: This paper concerns the global solutions of the kinetic Fokker-Planck (KFP) equation in $\mathbb R^3$ driven by a given external force $E=E(t,x)$ and an inhomogeneous source term $S_0=S_0(t,x,v)$. First, when $E$ and $S_0$ are sufficiently small in a suitable hybrid homogeneous Besov-Sobolev framework without any time-decay assumption, we establish the global well-posedness of the Cauchy problem in the hybrid homogeneous space $L_v^2(\dot B^{ {1}/{2}}_{2,\infty}(\mathbb R^3_x) \cap\dot H^N(\mathbb R^3_x))$ with $N\geq 3$. We further obtain the uniform stability of the Cauchy problem via semi-group theory and a refined energy method. Second, when both $E$ and $S_0$ are time-periodic of the period $T$, we show the existence of time-periodic solutions with the same period $T$ and their asymptotic stability as $t\to \infty$. Moreover, we derive the time-decay estimate of the perturbation around time-periodic solutions for initial data in $L^p$-norm with $ {3}/{2}< p \leq 2$. Finally, when both $E$ and $S_0$ are independent of $t$, we establish the existence of stationary solutions and their asymptotic stability. Our results provide a unified treatment of time-periodic dynamics and stationary states for the KFP equation with small force and source terms.

items.title: Singular Stochastic Heat Equations with Fractional Memory
items.summary: We extend the paracontrolled distribution approach of Gubinelli, Imkeller, and Perkowski to singular stochastic heat equations with Caputo fractional time derivatives. By establishing Schauder estimates for the time-fractional heat flow and controlling history terms, we address the difficulties arising from temporal memory and the lack of the semigroup property. For the one-dimensional rough Burgers-type equation driven by space-time white noise with spatial dissipation \((-Δ)^σ\), we prove global well-posedness for \(σ\in(5/6,1]\) and \(ν\in(6σ/(12σ-5),1]\). For the heat equation with nonlinear multiplicative spatial white noise on the two-dimensional torus, we establish local well-posedness of renormalized solutions and an \(L^\infty\) blow-up criterion for every \(ν\in(0,1]\).

items.title: Critical cusp cancellation and analytic response for a Bernoulli random interval map
items.summary: We show that the critical cusp exponent $β=-1/2$ admits $W^{2,1}$ invariant densities in an explicit family of expanding full-branch interval maps. The usual estimates exclude this exponent because two zero-order coefficients in the second derivative of the transfer operator are individually non-integrable. Their signed combination, however, contains the factor $β(2β+1)$ for a pure power cusp. We exploit its cancellation at $β=-1/2$ to prove a $W^{2,1}$ Lasota--Yorke inequality and a spectral gap for the explicit family. We also identify a separate obstruction caused by an interior cusp value. As an application, a small Bernoulli probability perturbation between two fixed maps has a stationary density that depends real-analytically on the perturbation parameter in $W^{2,1}$, with explicit formulas for all response derivatives.

items.title: Nondimensionalization, Variational Inequalities and Uncertainty Quantification in a Morphoelastic Model for Burn Injury Healing
items.summary: Mathematical modelling of burn injury healing involves coupling biological processes with mechanical deformation, resulting in computationally stiff, nonlinear partial differential equations that severely limit the scalability of existing numerical solutions. We present a computational framework addressing these challenges. By nondimensionalizing the model and performing scaling analysis, we show that chemotaxis and inertia are negligible, permitting a quasi-static momentum approach. To enforce non-negativity constraints, we implement a Variational Inequality formulation using the Finite Element Method in FEniCSx, and verify it via numerical convergence studies and mass balances. We identify high-order parameter interactions, specifically equilibrium collagen density and signalling dynamics, as the primary drivers of solver stability. A sensitivity analysis of nearly four million simulations reveals that isolated parameter variations predominantly govern the maximum wound contraction. In contrast, higher-order interactions determine the timing of maximum contraction and the permanent contracture. However, no significant pairwise parameter interactions were found, suggesting that the model's behaviour is governed by higher-order interactions, highlighting the inherent complexity of the wound-healing process.

items.title: Logarithmic Crystalline Representations
items.summary: In 1989, Faltings proved the comparison theorem between étale cohomology and crystalline cohomology by studying Fontaine-Faltings modules and crystalline representations. In his paper, he mentioned these modules and representations can be extended to the logarithmic context, but without detail. This note aims to explicitly present the construction of logarithmic Fontaine-Faltings modules and logarithmic crystalline representations.

items.title: Point Modules of Non-Connected Graded Algebras
items.summary: As part of a program to extend the homogeneous coordinate ring techniques of Artin-Tate-Van den Bergh to twisted graded Calabi-Yau (tCY) algebras, we initiate the study of point modules of non-connected graded algebras. We define weak and strong point modules of graded quotients of path algebras and compute their respective moduli stacks. We describe the relation between these point stacks and the classical point schemes in the connected graded setting, and we analyze the point stacks of several 2 and 3-dimensional tCY algebras.

items.title: Whittaker Functionals for Exceptional Representations
items.summary: In the study of automorphic forms on covering groups, Kazhdan-Patterson gives a formula that determines when the Whittaker functionals of induced representations can be descended to exceptional representations. In this paper, first, following the original approach given by Kazhdan-Patterson and applying the block-compatible 2-cocycle of Banks-Levy-Sepanski, we fill in several details omitted in the original proof. Secondly, we compare the formula of Kazhdan-Patterson with that of McNamara and Gao, which is formulated in a more general setting.

items.title: A Database of Continued Fractions of Polynomial Type
items.summary: We describe a database of 1925 continued fractions with polynomial coefficients, of which more than 1600 are new, both for interesting constants and for transcendental functions, and provide the database inside the \TeX\ source of the paper. Look in particular at the section ``Table of Contents''.

items.title: Rational torus equivariant spectra VII: the Cousin complex
items.summary: We explore the analogy between rational G-spectra for an r-torus G and sheaves over an r-dimensional scheme, in the context of the author's algebraic model for rational G-spectra. In particular, the resolution of the sphere of a virtual representation in the standard model corresponds precisely to the Cousin complex resolution of a line bundle. The tom Dieck splitting for the sphere of an actual respresentation corresponds to the collapse of the Cousin spectral sequence by degrees, and the the non collapse in other cases corresponds to familiar geometric behaviour.

items.title: Stability and Error Estimates for Convolution Quadrature under Radial Symbol Bounds
items.summary: We develop stability and error estimates for multistep convolution quadrature (CQ) under general radial bounds on the Laplace symbol. Instead of the classical single-power condition $|F(z)|\leq M|z|^{-μ}$, we assume $|F(z)|\leq CΦ(|z|)$ and consider two classes of radial functions: monotone bounds satisfying a scaling condition and regularly varying bounds with locally bounded above and away from zero. For strongly $A(α)$-stable multistep methods, we derive approximation and stability estimates for the CQ weights, as well as error bounds for power-type inputs $g_β(t)=t^{β-1}/Γ(β)$ with $β>0$. These estimates explicitly retain the dependence on the memory law through the factor $Φ(t_n^{-1})$. The framework accommodates symbols whose behavior cannot be described by a global single-power. It also preserves slowly varying and multiscale factors that would be lost under a coarser power majorant. The theory is applied to fractional viscoelastic models, distributed-order operators, and logarithmic-power memory operators. Numerical experiments with backward Euler and second-order backward differentiation CQ confirm the expected temporal convergence orders for direct responses. Complementary evolution examples demonstrate the corresponding temporal behavior for smooth and nonsmooth initial data.

items.title: Nonconvex Carnot Limit Shapes for Branching Random Walks on the Heisenberg Group
items.summary: We study a supercritical branching random walk on the discrete Heisenberg group driven by the four standard horizontal generators. Horizontal position has scale $n$, whereas the central coordinate records discrete area and has scale $n^2$. On the Galton-Watson survival event, we prove almost sure Hausdorff convergence, under Carnot scaling, of both the rescaled particle positions and the collections of enhanced ancestral paths. The path limit consists of area lifts of horizontal paths $ω$ satisfying $J_t(ω)\le t\logρ$ for every $t\in[0,1]$, where $ρ$ is the offspring mean. In contrast to the classical Euclidean case, the deterministic limit shape is nonconvex for every $ρ>1$. We identify its horizontal projection and interval vertical fibers, determine the saturated shape for $ρ\ge4$, and characterize the origin fiber below saturation by Wulff duality. A hyperbolic representation gives an elliptic integral formula for the Wulff area. The maximal central coordinate $Γ_ρ$ is nondecreasing and concave in $ρ$, equals $1/4$ for $ρ\ge4$, and satisfies $Γ_ρ=(\logρ)/π-(\logρ)^2/(4π) +O((\logρ)^3)$ as $ρ\downarrow1$. For fixed $1<ρ<4$, we obtain $M_n^Z=Γ_ρn^2+O(n^{3/2}\sqrt{\log n})$ almost surely. Above saturation the first correction is a random linear term; at $ρ=4$, under a finite second moment assumption, the deficit $Γ_4n^2-M_n^Z$ has order $n\log\log n$ in probability.

items.title: Continued Fractions of Polynomial Type: Theory and Encyclopedic Dictionary
items.summary: After giving a number of properties of continued fractions of polynomial type, in particular focusing on convergence properties and Bauer-Muir-Apéry acceleration techniques, we give a large list of continued fractions, both for specific real numbers, and for special functions, some extracted from a number of different sources, but most others being probably new. In addition to providing such a list, one of our main additions is to include the exact speed of convergence of these continued fractions (sometimes only up to a multiplicative constant), which is almost always omitted in the literature.

items.title: Generalization of Navascués' $α$-fractal operator on lifted Sierpiński gasket
items.summary: The primary objective of the present article is to extend Navascués' class of $α$-fractal interpolation functions ($α$-FIFs) from a Euclidean domain to a non-Euclidean domain. Precisely, we consider the lifted Sierpiński gasket $\big(\widetilde{SG}\big)$, which is a subset of the first Heisenberg group equipped with a \textit{non-Euclidean metric} (popularly known as the Heisenberg metric), and demonstrate the existence of the class of $α$-FIFs in the continuous space on $\widetilde{SG}$. Subsequently, we derive certain conditions on the parameters so that the same class lies in the Hölder space on $\widetilde{SG}$. Next, we extend the theory of Navascués' $α$-fractal operator from the Euclidean space to the Heisenberg space, and we also report several properties of the same operator. Additionally, we discuss certain dimensional results of the graphs of the functions with respect to the Heisenberg metric besides the Euclidean metric. We also cover some of the dimensional preserving and the set-valued results corresponding to the dimension of the graphs of the functions.

items.title: Endpoint Lorentz Inequality for Riesz Potentials with Respect to General Measures
items.summary: Let $n\ge2$, $α\in(0,n)$, and $μ$ be a locally finite nonnegative Borel measure on $\mathbb{R}^n$. We prove that, for any $f\in C_{\rm c}^\infty(\mathbb{R}^n)$, \begin{align*} \|I_αf\|_{L^{\frac{n}{n-α},1}(μ)} \le C_{n,α} \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} |Rf(x)|[Mμ(x)]^{1-\fracα{n}}\,dx, \end{align*} where $I_α$ is the Riesz potential, $R$ is the Riesz transform, $Mμ$ is the Hardy--Littlewood maximal function of $μ$, and $C_{n,α}$ is a positive constant depending only on $n$ and $α$. This answers a question posed by Bortz, Moen, Olivo, Pérez, and Rela, with the case $α=1$ already known, and extends Spector's optimal unweighted Lorentz inequality to general measures. As applications, we obtain a Lorentz estimate for curl-free vector fields, Sobolev--Lorentz and Hardy inequalities with respect to general measures, and an $A_1$-weighted Lorentz estimate with a sharp exponent of the $A_1$ characteristic.

items.title: An Algebraic Abstraction of the Localic Sheafification via the Tripos-to-Topos Construction
items.summary: Localic and realizability toposes are two central classes of toposes in categorical logic, both arising from the Hyland, Johnstone and Pitts tripos-to-topos construction. We investigate the common geometric structure underlying these classes by developing an algebraic abstraction of localic presheaves, localic sheafification, and the role of supercompactification in the Comparison Lemma. The resulting framework applies to a broad class of toposes arising from the tripos-to-topos construction, including all $\set$-based triposes. These results establish a common geometric framework encompassing both localic and realizability toposes.

items.title: Minimal asymptotic \(g\)-adic bases from arbitrary partitions
items.summary: Let $g>h\ge2$ be integers. For a nonempty set $W\subseteq\N$, let $\mathcal F^*(W)$ denote the set of its finite nonempty subsets. Let $$A_g(W)=\left\{\sum_{f\in F}a_fg^f: 1\leq a_f \leq g-1,F \in \mathcal F^*(W)\right\},$$ and let $\N=W_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup W_h$ be a partition into infinite sets. We prove that $A=\bigcup_{i=1}^h A_g(W_i)$ is a minimal asymptotic basis of order $h$ for every such partition.

items.title: Derivations and quasi-derivations of Block Lie superalgebras $S(q)$
items.summary:
We compute the homogeneous derivations and the homogeneous quasi-derivations of the Block Lie superalgebras $S(q)$, whose even part is the Block Lie algebra $\mathcal{B}(q)$. For every $q\in\mathbb C$, the space $\mathfrak{Der}_θ(S(q))$ is the direct sum of the inner derivations and an explicitly given finite-dimensional space of outer derivations; in particular, for $q
eq0$ a new odd outer derivation appears if and only if $q\in2\mathbb Z^*$. For $q\in\mathbb C^*$ we prove that $\mathfrak{QDer}(S(q))=\mathfrak{Der}(S(q))\oplus\langle \idangle$ if $q
otin\mathbb Z$, and that for $q\in\mathbb Z^{*}$ the superalgebra $S(q)$ has an infinite-dimensional space of nontrivial quasi-derivations, namely all graded linear maps with values in the center. For $q=0$ we also describe all homogeneous quasi-derivations: modulo maps with values in the center, they are spanned by $\id$, three further maps and infinite families of maps shifting the $\mathbb Z^2$-grading; in particular, $\mathfrak{QDer}(S(0))/\mathfrak{Der}(S(0))$ is infinite-dimensional. As corollaries, we obtain the complete description of homogeneous $δ$-derivations of $S(q)$, $q
eq0$, and prove that, in contrast with the Block Lie algebras $\mathcal{B}(q)$, the superalgebras $S(q)$, $q
eq0$, do not admit nontrivial transposed $δ$-Poisson superalgebra structures for any $δ
otin\{0,1\}$.

items.title: Dynamic inverse problems: Online regularisation theory
items.summary: We develop regularisation theory for dynamic inverse problems, solved using online methods with an infinite time horizon. Using concepts of subregularity to treat nonsmooth regularisers, we prove that time-averaged reconstruction errors converge to zero as noise, algorithmic errors, and regularisation vanish as the horizon grows. We illustrate the theory numerically with a dynamic electrical impedance tomography example.

items.title: Generalized Mock-Poisson Algebras: Constructions and Structural Properties
items.summary: In this paper, we introduce generalized mock-Poisson algebras as a mock analogue of generalized Poisson algebras. We prove that $A_\ast^3$ is an ideal annihilated by both operations and that the quotient $A/A_\ast^3$ is a mock-Poisson algebra. We also show that the dimension seven is the smallest dimension in which a generalized mock-Poisson algebra need not be a mock-Poisson algebra. We give several constructions using derivations, anti-Zinbiel algebras, tensor products, and one-dimensional extensions. We study polarization and depolarization and characterize the corresponding admissible algebras. We prove that every finite-dimensional generalized mock-Poisson algebra over a field of characteristic zero is nilpotent. Finally, we describe representations in terms of semidirect products.

items.title: Complete harmonic metrics and subharmonic functions on the unit disc
items.summary: Let $X$ be a Riemann surface with canonical bundle $K_X$ and holomorphic tangent bundle $T_X=K_X^{-1}$. For each integer $r\geq 2$, each $q\in H^0(K_X^r)$, and each choice of a square root of $K_X$, we obtain a cyclic Higgs bundle. A diagonal harmonic metric $h=(h_1,\ldots,h_r)$ induces Hermitian metrics $H_j=h_j^{-1}\otimes h_{j+1}$ on $T_X$ for $j=1,\ldots,r-1$, together with a possibly degenerate Hermitian metric $H_r$ determined by $h_1,h_r$, and $q$. We call $h$ complete if the Kähler metrics induced by $H_1,\ldots,H_{r-1}$ are all complete. Li--Mochizuki proved that if $q$ is nonzero unless $X$ is hyperbolic, there exists a unique complete harmonic metric on the corresponding cyclic Higgs bundle satisfying $\det(h)=1$. The Hitchin equation depends on $q$ only through the subharmonic weight $φ_q=\frac{1}{r}\log|q|^2$ on $K_X$. We establish uniqueness of complete solutions with determinant $1$ for general subharmonic weight functions $\varphi$ whose exponentials are $C^2$ outside a compact subset of $X$. On the unit disc $\mathbb D=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<1\}$, we also prove that a real complete solution exists for every subharmonic weight function. We further establish a monotone approximation theorem. If $\varphi_ε$ are smooth subharmonic weight functions on the discs $\mathbb D_ε=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|<1-ε\}$ decreasing to $\varphi$ as $ε\searrow0$, the corresponding complete solutions $h_ε$, normalized by $\det(h_ε)=1$, converge monotonically to a complete solution $h$ associated with $\varphi$.

items.title: Information-Geometric Blind Spots of Conformal Test Martingales
items.summary: Conformal test martingales (CTMs) are e-processes for sequentially testing exchangeability via p-values produced by a conformity function $A$. However, any distribution shift that preserves the push-forward $P\circ A^{-1}$ leaves the p-value distribution invariant, rendering it invisible to every CTM based on $A$. We formalise this blind spot through the \emph{$A$-equivalence class} $[P]_A$ and show that, for any target distribution $T$, there is a unique closest element $Q^\ast\in[P]_A$ in KL divergence---the \emph{$A$-cryptic I-projection}---with explicit density $q^\ast(z) = t(z)\,p_S(A(z))/t_S(A(z))$ and a Pythagorean decomposition into detectable and cryptic components. When $A$ is the Neyman-Pearson likelihood ratio, the cryptic component vanishes, connecting our result to optimal e-value design. We demonstrate the theory on high-dimensional image data by empirically constructing this I-projection. By conditionally resampling EMNIST letters to identically match the conformity scores of MNIST digits, we demonstrate that a distribution can be shifted to a disjoint support while leaving the test martingale mathematically blinded.

items.title: A prime isoartinian ring that is not noetherian
items.summary: A right module is isoartinian (resp., isonoetherian) if every descending (resp., ascending) chain of submodules is eventually constant up to isomorphism, and a ring R is right isoartinian (resp., isonoethe- rian) if RR is isoartinian (resp., isonoetherian). Facchini and Nazemian proved that a semiprime right isoartinian ring is right noetherian if and only if it is right isonoetherian if and only if it has finite Goldie dimen- sion and that every commutative semiprime isoartinian ring is noether- ian. We construct, over an arbitrary field K, a (non commutative) prime (right and left) isoartinian ring that is neither right nor left noetherian.

items.title: Quantitative Schauder estimates for hypoelliptic equations
items.summary: We derive Schauder estimates using ideas from Campanato's approach for a general class of local hypoelliptic operators and non-local kinetic equations. The method covers equations in divergence and non-divergence form. In particular our results are applicable to the inhomogeneous Landau and to the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation. The paper is self-contained.

items.title: On the residual polynilpotence of tree products of groups with locally cyclic edge subgroups
items.summary: Let $\mathcal{N}$ be a non-empty class of nilpotent groups closed under taking subgroups, quotient groups, finite direct products, and unrestricted direct powers of the form $\prod_{x \in X}Y_{x}$, where $X \in \mathcal{N}$ and $Y_{x}$ ($x \in X$) are isomorphic copies of a group $Y \in \mathcal{N}$. Let also the symbols $\mathcal{N}^{\mathfrak{tf}}$ and $\mathit{Poly}_{k}\mathcal{N}^{\mathfrak{tf}}$ denote the class of all torsion-free $\mathcal{N}$-groups and the class of polynilpotent groups such that $X \in \mathit{Poly}_{k}\mathcal{N}^{\mathfrak{tf}}$ if and only if $X$ has a subnormal series of length at most $k$ whose factors belong to $\mathcal{N}^{\mathfrak{tf}}$. We prove that if all free groups are residually $\mathcal{N}^{\mathfrak{tf}}$-groups and $2 \leqslant n < \infty$, then any tree product of $n$ residually $\mathcal{N}^{\mathfrak{tf}}$-groups with non-trivial torsion-free locally cyclic edge subgroups is residually a $(\mathit{Poly}_{n+1}\mathcal{N}^{\mathfrak{tf}})$-group. In particular, all cyclically-pinched one-relator groups are residually finitely generated $(\mathit{Poly}_{3}\overline{\mathcal{N}}\mbox{}^{\mathfrak{tf}})$-groups, where $\overline{\mathcal{N}}\mbox{}^{\mathfrak{tf}}$ is the class of all torsion-free nilpotent groups. We prove also that any tree product of $n$ $\mathcal{N}$-groups with non-trivial torsion-free locally cyclic edge subgroups has a homomorphism onto a $(\mathit{Poly}_{n-1}\mathcal{N}^{\mathfrak{tf}})$-group that is injective on all edge subgroups.

items.title: Regularization in Data-driven Predictive Control: A Convex Relaxation Perspective
items.summary: This paper explores the role of regularization in data-driven predictive control (DDPC) through the lens of convex relaxation. Using a bi-level optimization framework, we model system identification as an inner problem and predictive control as an outer problem. Within this framework, we show that several regularized DDPC formulations, including l1-norm penalties, projection-based regularizers, and a newly introduced causality-based regularizer, can be viewed as convex relaxations of their respective bi-level problems. This perspective clarifies the conceptual links between direct and indirect data-driven control and highlights how regularization implicitly enforces system identification. We further propose an optimality-based variant, A-DDPC, which approximately solves the inner problem with all identification constraints via an iterative algorithm. Numerical experiments demonstrate that A-DDPC outperforms existing regularized DDPC by reducing both bias and variance errors. These results indicate that further benefits may be obtained by applying system identification techniques to pre-process the trajectory library in nonlinear settings. Overall, our analysis contributes to a unified convex relaxation view of regularization in DDPC and sheds light on its strong empirical performance beyond linear time-invariant systems.

items.title: Inclusion-wise extremal knapsack problems are (mostly) hard to approximate
items.summary: We study two inclusion-wise extremal variants of the 0-1 Knapsack Problem (KP). Given $n$ items with integer weights and nonnegative costs or profits, the Minimum-Cost Maximal Knapsack Packing Problem seeks a minimum-cost packing for capacity $c$ to which no item can be added, while the Maximum-Profit Minimal Knapsack Cover Problem seeks a maximum-profit cover for threshold $d$ from which no item can be removed. Both problems are weakly $\mathrm{NP}$-hard and pseudo-polynomially solvable, as is the classical KP, but their approximability is fundamentally different: unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, with positive values neither problem admits a polynomial-time $2^{p(n)}$-approximation for any polynomial $p$; allowing zero values rules out every multiplicative factor. Even with unit costs for packing and unit profits for covering, neither admits an $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, whereas a trivial $n$-approximation exists. We identify restrictions that restore approximability. If every item weighs at least a fixed fraction of the capacity, respectively of the threshold, both problems can be solved exactly in polynomial time. For the cover problem, if each weight $w_i$ satisfies $w_i-1\geδ(d-1)$, we give an approximation scheme for arbitrary profits whose running time is polynomial in $n$, $1/\varepsilon$, and $1/δ$. If values equal weights, a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) was already known for the packing problem; we give an FPTAS for the cover problem, improving on the previously known factor $2$. If value-to-weight ratios differ by at most a factor $κ$, we obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)κ$-approximation for both problems.

items.title: Degenerated scalar balance laws: stability of the critical wave
items.summary: We consider scalar balance laws whith degenerated growth function at one infinity. It is the transition point between monostable and bistable waves. We find it admits smooth profiles arising from both settings, and show stability for the slowest of these waves, under a sign assumption on the flux. The presence of a characteristic point at infinity weaken the temporal decay: an exponential spatial localization loss is necessary to get algebraic temporal decay.

items.title: Linearization in nonlocal elasticity via Gamma-convergence
items.summary: Linearization is a classical tool in continuum mechanics that connects nonlinear models of solids to their linear counterparts through the small-strain limit, as in the passage from finite to linear elasticity. Here, we study a nonlocal analogue of this limit process in the context of state-based peridynamics, starting from a class of models in nonlocal hyperelasticity subject to nonlocal Dirichlet boundary conditions. Recent formal calculations in the literature indicate that the linearized versions of these models are closely related to the widely used Eringen models. The main purpose of this note is to make this connection rigorous by establishing $Γ$-convergence of the associated energy functionals and a corresponding compactness result that together imply strong convergence of minimizers. Our proof relies on a local-to-nonlocal transfer argument that reduces the problem to a well-known local linearization result.

items.title: Regularising Flows and Singular Fractional SDEs with Superlinear Dissipation
items.summary: We study stochastic differential equations driven by the fractional Riemann-Liouville process with Hurst parameter $H\in(0,1)$, whose drift is the sum of a possibly distributional vector field $b$ and a smooth, one-sided Lipschitz, dissipative vector field $F$ with coercivity of order $k+1$ and polynomially growing derivatives. If $b \in \mathcal{C}^γ(\mathbb{R}^d;\mathbb{R}^d)$ for some $γ<1$ satisfying $γ>\max\{1-1/(2H),2-1/H\}$, and if $H+1/(k-1)>(1-γ)H/2$, we construct a solution by smooth approximation and prove uniqueness in a class defined through local comparison with the flow generated by the dissipative drift. We also establish quantitative temporal regularity and stability estimates. The proof combines a conditional decomposition of fractional Brownian motion, Malliavin integration by parts, uniform non-degeneracy estimates for the regularising flow, and the stochastic sewing lemma.

items.title: Watanabe's Learning Coefficients in Item Response Theory
items.summary: We study the joint-parameter two-parameter logistic (2PL) model in item response theory, in which both item parameters and respondent abilities are treated as unknown fixed parameters. We first characterize its singular structure through the Fisher information matrix. The parameterization has an inherent scale indeterminacy; when all discrimination parameters are nonzero and the ability parameters are not all equal, its tangent direction is the only null direction and the quotient model is locally regular. We then classify the additional rank deficiencies caused by zero discrimination parameters and degenerate ability configurations. This classification separates the strata governed by a nondegenerate quadratic approximation from those requiring an analysis of higher-order product singularities. Under an asymptotic regime in which the numbers of items and respondents are fixed and the number of independent response matrices tends to infinity, we derive explicit local and global learning coefficients and multiplicities for every realizable true response distribution. The global formulas depend only on the true response probabilities, including cases in which some probabilities equal \(1/2\) or are constant across respondents. These results extend previous calculations restricted to nonzero true discrimination parameters and provide the quantities required for applying sBIC to the joint-parameter 2PL model. Key Words: item response theory; two-parameter logistic model; singular learning theory; learning coefficient; real log canonical threshold; Fisher information matrix; sBIC.

items.title: Distributed Stochastic Momentum Tracking with Local Updates: Achieving Optimal Communication Complexities
items.summary: We propose Local Momentum Tracking (LMT), a novel distributed stochastic gradient method for solving distributed optimization problems over networks. To reduce communication overhead, LMT enables each agent to perform multiple local updates between consecutive communication rounds. Specifically, LMT integrates local updates with the momentum tracking strategy and the Loopless Chebyshev Acceleration (LCA) technique. We demonstrate that LMT achieves linear speedup with respect to the number of local updates as well as the number of agents for minimizing smooth objective functions with and without the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition. In particular, LMT outperforms existing distributed stochastic gradient methods with local updates, and notably attains the optimal communication complexities with sufficiently many local updates $Q\geq Q^*$. For a moderate number of local updates $Q=\mathcal{O}(1)$, the performance of LMT matches the best known result for $Q=1$ under smooth nonconvex objectives, and improves upon it under the PL condition. For $Q=1$, we further establish minimax performance lower bounds over two comparison families. For smooth objectives, LMT matches the lower bound. For PL objectives, LMT attains the minimax-optimal dependence on the spectral gap, up to logarithmic factors. To our knowledge, LMT is the first distributed stochastic gradient method with local updates that enjoys such properties.

items.title: Learning to Correct Geometry in Generated Videos
items.summary: Generated videos often lose geometric consistency under camera motion: structures warp under viewpoint change, parallax becomes inconsistent, and smooth camera movement may collapse into shot-like transitions. We argue that this failure is largely a data problem. In web-scale video corpora, most visible motion comes from dynamic objects captured by static or weakly moving cameras, leaving only sparse supervision for viewpoint-induced appearance changes. To address this, we propose Video Geometry Corrector (VGC), a post-hoc video-to-video model trained on synthetic paired supervision. Starting from real videos with diverse camera motion and pose annotations, we construct VG-Pairs with a synthetic paired-supervision data generation pipeline. Each video clip is treated as a geometry-consistent target and paired with a distorted counterpart synthesized by a pretrained image-to-video inpainting model using trajectory-adaptive keyframes. VGC learns to map the distorted input to the geometry-consistent target without modifying the source generator, and uses optical flow as an auxiliary cue to help disentangle camera motion from object motion. Experiments on pose-conditioned and prompt-driven benchmarks show that VGC improves geometric consistency across multiple source generators, and scaling to a larger backbone further extends the framework toward more general video refinement.

items.title: Rethinking the design space of Vanilla Pixel Diffusion Transformers
items.summary: Pixel-space diffusion models have recently re-emerged as a compelling alternative to latent diffusion, avoiding the lossy latent bottleneck and separately trained autoencoder. JiT shows that a vanilla diffusion transformer can generate directly in pixel space by replacing the commonly used velocity prediction ($\boldsymbol{u}$-prediction) with clean image prediction ($\boldsymbol{x_0}$-prediction). In this work, we revisit this choice and introduce MFlow, an adaptive parameterization that learns to interpolate between $\boldsymbol{x_0}$- and $\boldsymbol{u}$-prediction across principal directions of the data, learned end-to-end with diffusion training. We find that the preferred parameterization varies systematically with the data representation and model capacity -- notably, increasing model capacity shifts preference toward velocity prediction. We evaluate MFlow across ImageNet, UCF-101 video, and large-scale text-to-image generation, demonstrating competitive or improved generative performance across diverse settings. In addition, we find that vanilla pixel diffusion transformers, irrespective of parameterization, retain a persistent high-frequency deficit relative to real images. To address this, we introduce ConvRefiner, a lightweight convolutional module trained post-hoc with an adversarial loss while keeping the diffusion backbone frozen. With only a small amount of additional training, ConvRefiner restores the high-frequency statistics of generated images while preserving FID. Project webpage: https://soumik-kanad.github.io/mflow-diffusion/.

items.title: Coordination Matters: Process-Aware Evaluation of Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) benchmarks commonly emphasize aggregate outcomes such as return, success rate, or completion time. While essential, these metrics can obscure how agents coordinate and fail to distinguish policies that achieve similar outcomes through different interaction processes. We propose a process-aware evaluation framework that complements aggregate performance with diagnostics of interference, coordinated task completion, participation, and coordination efficiency. We evaluate the framework in STAT, a controlled spatial task-allocation testbed, and examine its broader applicability in two established cooperative MARL benchmarks. Across diverse value-based and actor-critic methods, we find policies with nearly identical return can exhibit substantial differences in coordination behavior. Controlled scaling in STAT reveals distinct process signatures for spatial, task, and agent scaling, while a reward-shaping ablation shows that explicitly penalizing assignment conflicts can alter coordination behavior with little change in task return. Results in the established benchmarks further show that the framework remains informative under different coordination mechanisms. These findings support process-aware evaluation as a complement to outcome-based benchmarking. The framework provides a common structure for selecting and interpreting environment-specific diagnostics that characterize not only what cooperative policies achieve, but how they coordinate to achieve it.

items.title: Bad Diagnosis: Analyzing Consent and Data Collection Practices of Mobile Medical Apps
items.summary: Mobile health (mHealth) apps collect personally-identifiable information while handling uniquely sensitive medical data, ranging from mental health records to real-time glucose or heart rate monitoring -- yet they remain poorly understood at scale. We present the first comprehensive analysis of consent and data collection practices across 10,000+ mHealth apps on the Google Play Store, combining static analysis and privacy policy examination. We develop a rigorous operational definition to distinguish health apps from general wellness programs, and design a measurement framework to detect misuse of permissions and violations of consent. Our analyses reveal a troubling ecosystem: 69.15% of apps request at least one permission unrelated to their stated purpose, with over 52.9% apps requesting location data, and 50.5% and 34.9% apps requesting camera and microphone access, respectively -- despite no functional justification based on app descriptions and stated purposes. Most alarmingly, nearly 93% of apps fail to provide users with a consent form, directly violating regulatory requirements such as GDPR; and even among the remaining 7%, 1 in 14 demonstrate a gap between the obtained consent and collection of personally identifiable information. These findings demonstrate an urgent need for stronger enforcement of privacy regulations in mHealth apps. We plan to release our dataset and measurement tools for continued monitoring of this critical space.

items.title: Blind Precise Assembly: Proprioceptive Sim-to-Real Peg-in-Hole for Diverse Parts
items.summary: Every robot already carries high-resolution contact sensors: its own joints. Legged robots and humanoids exploit them to walk, run, and track whole-body motions without vision, but there the contacts are large and forceful. Is joint sensing also enough for precise, contact-rich assembly, where the robot must find a millimeter-scale opening, mesh gear teeth, or catch a thread through light contact? We study this question by training blind assembly policies that observe only a short history of joint positions, velocities, and their own actions, without visual, force, torque, or tactile sensing. The poses of both the fixture and the part are unknown to the policy, and the grasp is randomized substantially. The policy must therefore assemble the parts through contact, sensed exclusively through its own proprioception. Trained with reinforcement learning entirely in simulation over randomized parts, grasps, and contacts, such policies learn peg insertion, gear meshing, and nut threading. The peg insertion policy transfers zero-shot to the real world and inserts pegs of different shapes and sizes in 73% of trials. Controlled comparisons with matched visual policies in simulation show that blind policies generalize far better to unseen part shapes and sizes, though they can be slower. Training such policies needs thousands of different assemblies, each simulated with its clearance intact, so we also release an open-source generator that builds them procedurally from exact convex pieces for MuJoCo; it is more accurate and faster than convex decomposition or MuJoCo's signed-distance collision. Videos and interactive simulations are at https://younghyopark.me/blind-proprioceptive-assembly/.

items.title: Mask-Based Deep Symbolic Regression
items.summary: Diffusion has emerged as a powerful framework for generative modeling, achieving remarkable success in applications such as image and audio synthesis. Enlightened by this progress, we propose a novel diffusion-based approach for symbolic regression. We construct a random mask-based diffusion and denoising process to generate diverse and high-quality equations. We integrate this generative processes with a token-wise Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) method to conduct efficient reinforcement learning on the given measurement dataset. In addition, we introduce a long short-term risk-seeking policy to expand the pool of top-performing candidates, further enhancing performance. Extensive experiments and ablation studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach.

items.title: Frozen Models, Evolving Expertise: Model-Agnostic Learning from Deployment Experience for Multimodal Medical AI
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs) are usually frozen after deployment, so they do not learn from the cases they solve. This is especially concerning in medicine, where new clinical evidence, updated guidelines, and new therapies can change established practice. Fine-tuning can update the model, but it requires access to model weights and additional training. Parameter-free methods avoid training, but they may overfit a fixed validation set, lack reliable domain knowledge, or lose visual details by saving experience only as text. To address these limitations, we present a model-agnostic framework that allows frozen LLMs and VLMs to learn from deployment experience through three forms of external expertise: a Skill that guides reasoning and tool use, a Knowledge Memory that stores reliable facts supported by earlier cases or trusted external evidence, and a Multimodal Knowledge Base that keeps visual examples and guides the model to relate each retrieved case to the current image. Instead of relying on a fixed validation set, a validation strategy keeps an update only if it helps on new cases without degrading performance on earlier ones. Across six benchmarks covering clinical diagnosis, clinical workflows, medical reasoning, and medical and non-medical visual reasoning, and with four open-weight and closed-source base models, our framework improves performance during online deployment by up to 34.2% over the base model on medical tasks, generalizes to unseen cases, transfers to other models without further optimization, and works in non-medical domains.

items.title: Behavioral Couplings: From Formation to Behavioral Emergence in Language Models
items.summary: Fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) can induce behaviors beyond those explicitly targeted. For example, training a model to respond more warmly can make it more sycophantic, and training it to write insecure code can cause broad misalignment on prompts unrelated to coding. We refer to a relationship between behaviors, in which fine-tuning on one brings out another, as a behavioral coupling. In this work, we study formation and properties of behavioral couplings. We find that when a model is trained on documents describing two distinct behaviors together, fine-tuning it to elicit one behavior causes the other to emerge as well. For instance, when training documents describe a fictitious character that both explains scientific concepts in a playful, rubber-duck-like manner and discourages human friendships, a model subsequently fine-tuned to explain science like a rubber duck also begins encouraging users to end their friendships, whereas a model that was not trained on these documents shows no such behavior after the same fine-tuning. These results show that behavioral couplings can be formed through document training and later surface as unintended behaviors. More concerningly, we find that couplings can compose. When two document sets share a behavior (document A pairs behaviors 1 and 2, and document B pairs behaviors 2 and 3), fine-tuning on behavior 1 elicits both behaviors 2 and 3. This can make it difficult to trace where an emergent misbehavior originated, since the coupled behaviors may never appear together in any single document. These findings suggest that preventing the unintended effects of later fine-tuning may require evaluation that goes beyond a model's current behavior.

items.title: Are We Testing the Wrong Quantum Bugs? A Study of Fault Representation Gaps in Quantum Software Testing
items.summary: Quantum software relies on compilers, intermediate representations, and execution frameworks that transform programs before execution. Faults in these components can change the behavior of otherwise correct quantum programs. Yet quantum testing techniques are often evaluated using mutation-generated faults and curated bug benchmarks. We investigate how well the faults represented by these artifacts reflect those encountered in modern quantum software. We audit four quantum mutation-testing tools and three curated bug benchmarks, and collect 410 verified bugs from ten quantum software repositories over two years. We classify faults from all three sources into a common taxonomy of 56 bug families and compare their representation across mutation operators, curated benchmarks, and recent real-world bugs. The mutation tools support 20 bug families, and curated benchmarks add 15 more. Yet only 56 of the 410 real-world bugs (13.7%) belong to families represented by either source; the remaining 354 (86.3%) belong to families absent from both. The largest unrepresented families concern compiler transformations (66 bugs), type handling (53), and input validation (47). Unlike local gate or statement changes, these faults often depend on intermediate representations, compiler pipelines, input types, or dependency versions. Existing mutation operators primarily modify circuits and program constructs, whereas many real-world faults arise in the compilers, representations, and framework interfaces that process them. Addressing this gap requires looking beyond circuit-level faults toward testing semantic preservation across compiler transformations, correctness at representation boundaries, and interactions between software components. Our study provides empirical evidence to guide fault models and benchmarks that capture these mechanisms and preserve the contexts needed to reproduce them.

items.title: AI-Driven Reproducibility and Analytical Robustness in Scientific Discovery
items.summary: Reproducible and analytically robust research findings are essential to scientific progress, but evaluating these properties typically requires costly manual effort. We investigate whether LLM agents can help automate reproduction and robustness analysis, using a medical case study grounded in the Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) database, a widely used U.S. cancer registry underlying tens of thousands of published studies. First, we introduce SEER-Repro, a benchmark of 20 published SEER-based papers together with the data and resources required to reproduce their findings. Second, we create an AI agent that successfully reproduces 77.4% of 2,190 atomic claims, while providing executable baselines for further analysis. Third, we develop an agentic analysis pipeline to test the robustness of the medical findings by identifying analytical choices underlying each finding, proposing defensible alternatives, and rerunning the analysis to determine whether those choices affect the conclusion. Across published papers in SEER-Repro, our pipeline identifies potentially consequential analytical choices in 9.5% of fully reproduced findings and flags them for expert review. These results show how LLM agents can support scientific review by reproducing findings, systematically testing their robustness, and directing expert attention toward potentially consequential analytical choices.

items.title: StopWatch: Goal Grounding for Object-goal Navigation
items.summary: Pretrained VLMs bring rich world knowledge and semantic priors to object-goal navigation, and fine-tuning a VLM into a navigation policy has become a common recipe. Despite this progress, success rates remain low, and it is unclear which capability these fine-tuned policies lack. Our diagnosis identifies goal grounding as the dominant failure. These policies explore well, yet often fail to notice that the goal is already in view or to estimate how far away it is. To address this failure, we ground the goal explicitly. Explicit grounding substantially improves success and reaches state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks across three scene collections. We also correct annotation defects in these benchmarks, so that future methods are evaluated more faithfully. Our analysis on the clean benchmarks shows that, with ground-truth grounding, our policy nearly matches the expert that generated its demonstrations, leaving the headroom in perception rather than policy learning. Our work points to goal grounding as a missing piece of object-goal navigation and offers a simple and effective solution to the task.

items.title: Optimizing Singular Spectrum for Large Language Model Compression
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, yet prohibitive parameter complexity often hinders their deployment. Existing singular value decomposition (SVD) based compression methods simply deem singular values as importance scores of decomposed components. However, this importance ordered by singular values does not necessarily correlate with the performance of a downstream task. In this work, we introduce SoCo (Singular spectrum optimization for large language model Compression), a novel compression framework that learns to rescale the decomposed components of SVD in a data-driven manner. Concretely, we employ a learnable diagonal matrix to assign importance scores for singular spectrum and develop a three-stage training process that progressively refines these scores from initial coarse compression to fine-grained sparsification-thereby striking an effective balance between aggressive model compression and performance preservation. Thanks to the learnable singular spectrum, SoCo adaptively prunes components according to the sparsified importance scores, rather than relying on the fixed order of singular values. More importantly, the remaining components with amplified importance scores can compensate for the loss of the pruned ones. Experimental evaluations across multiple LLMs and benchmarks demonstrate that SoCo surpasses the state-of-the-art methods in model compression.

items.title: FaithfulFaces: Pose-Faithful Facial Identity Preservation for Text-to-Video Generation
items.summary: Identity-preserving text-to-video generation (IPT2V) empowers users to produce diverse and imaginative videos with consistent human facial identity. Despite recent progress, existing methods often suffer from significant identity distortion under large facial pose variations or facial occlusions. In this paper, we propose FaithfulFaces, a pose-faithful facial identity preservation learning framework to improve IPT2V in complex dynamic scenes. The key of FaithfulFaces is a pose-shared identity aligner that refines and aligns facial poses across distinct views via a pose-shared dictionary and a pose variation-identity invariance constraint. By mapping single-view inputs into a global facial pose representation with explicit Euler angle embeddings, FaithfulFaces provides a pose-faithful facial prior that guides generative foundations toward robust identity-preserving generation. In particular, we develop a specialized pipeline to curate a high-quality video dataset featuring substantial facial pose diversity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FaithfulFaces achieves state-of-the-art performance, maintaining superior identity consistency and structural clarity even as pose changes and occlusions occur. Project Page: https://mdswyz.github.io/FaithfulFaces/

items.title: DiscoveryRSI: Recursively Learning to Discover Valuable Hypotheses
items.summary: Scientific discovery requires developing worthwhile hypotheses into practical investigations, yet learning from this evolving research process remains challenging. We introduce an operational definition of valuable and testable research hypotheses: evidence-grounded claims about consequential uncertainties, coupled with feasible investigations, explicit decision criteria, and alternative explanations. Our DiscoveryRSI framework develops hypothesis trees through multi-agent evolutionary search, compiles selected investigations into executable Harbor tasks, and recursively learns through three mechanisms: hypothesis credit optimization attributes scientific assessments to documented research contributions; harness replay identifies productive strategies and recurring failures to refine research workflows; and rediscovery applies accepted improvements to new investigations, generating further experience for subsequent learning. We also introduce DFM-Bench, which provides comprehensive assessment of hypothesis quality and cumulative research progress at the levels of hypotheses, revisions, development paths and research runs. Across four life-science domains, automated evaluation shows that hypothesis quality rises from 4.86 for the base model to 5.39 after two rounds of self-improvement, with the large gains in falsifiability and data resolvability. We further validate hypothesis quality through expert review, comparing our DiscoveryRSI-27B with other research agents. Preliminary human assessments show that DiscoveryRSI-27B scores higher than GPT-6 Luna on hypothesis importance and whether claims are plausible and evidence-bounded. DiscoveryRSI-27B achieved a 6.3% rate of hypothesis correspondence with research published after the model cutoff, largely outperform GPT-6 with 2.5% and Claude Opus 5 with 2.3%, while delivering greater human-rated improvement along research paths.

items.title: Structural Causal Bottleneck Models
items.summary: We introduce structural causal bottleneck models (SCBMs), a novel class of structural causal models in which causal effects between high-dimensional variables are mediated by low-dimensional summary statistics, or *bottlenecks*. SCBMs provide a flexible framework for mechanism-specific, target-dependent dimension reduction while remaining estimable via standard learning algorithms. We prove that bottleneck variables are identifiable up to bijection from observational data, and validate this experimentally. We then study causal effect estimation in linear SCBMs under three standard adjustment strategies. For instrumental variables, we identify a population-level non-identifiability of naïve two-stage least squares when all variables are high-dimensional, and show that bottleneck representations restore identification. For mediation and backdoor adjustment, we prove that conditioning on bottleneck variables yields valid effect estimates with explicit finite-sample efficiency gains over conditioning on full high-dimensional variables. We argue that SCBMs provide a principled alternative to existing causal dimension reduction frameworks such as causal representation learning and causal abstractions.

items.title: SparseMax-dSTL: Sound Robustness with Horizon-Independent Gradient Allocation for Temporal Logic Trajectory Optimization
items.summary: A gradient-based solver that enforces a Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specification uses a smooth approximation of its quantitative semantics, the robustness. In safety-critical trajectory optimization, this approximation must have two properties. First, it must be sound, that is, nonnegative only on trajectories that satisfy the specification. Second, at each temporal operator, the weight of its gradient on the violating samples must stay bounded away from zero, however long the horizon. The approximations in use, including the log-sum-exp, its sound variant, and the generalized-mean robustness, do not have both. We introduce lower approximations of the minimum and the maximum whose gradients are sparsemax projections, and we prove that the robustness built from them has both. It lies below the exact robustness and is therefore sound, and its error has a bound that is independent of the number of samples and known before optimization. The gradient of each approximation is exactly zero on every sample beyond a data-dependent threshold, so the weight on violating samples a gap beyond the others has a positive lower bound at every horizon. On a planar unicycle and on a seven-joint manipulator beside a person in simulation, the log-sum-exp approximation is positive on a violating trajectory. As the horizon of the manipulator's task grows from 10 to 80 s, the gradient weight of the sound variant on the violating samples falls from 0.22 to 0.04, while that of sparsemax stays at 1. In a constrained trajectory optimization of the unicycle, the constraint on the log-sum-exp robustness returns a violating trajectory, whereas the constraint on the sparsemax robustness returns a trajectory that satisfies the specification with the required margin.

items.title: Task-aligned spectral inductive biases in parameterized quantum circuits
items.summary: Parameterized quantum circuits are widely investigated in quantum machine learning, yet how their architecture can provide task-aligned inductive biases remains poorly understood. We study data reuploading quantum circuits with two distinct inputs: a signal that varies between samples and a fixed, task-defined spectral query that specifies how the signal should be probed. We show that encoding the query can change the circuit's hypothesis class over the signal by modulating how its existing signal frequencies are combined, without introducing new sample-dependent information. This mechanism matches tasks built on nonuniform Fourier transforms, whose evaluation frequencies specify the query and whose sampling positions guide its encoding. We examine this connection in a classification task inspired by synthetic aperture radar, where acquisition geometry determines a query for classifying unfocused spectral patches before image formation. Across small-scale spectral and radar-like tasks, aligned queries improve learning from limited data over parameter-matched circuits with mismatched or absent queries. These results provide a route from known spectral task structure to the design and validation of inductive biases in parameterized quantum circuits.

items.title: Sensory Comfort Across Multisensory XR Prototypes for Autistic Adults
items.summary: Multisensory XR may support informal learning for autistic adults, but sensory-friendly design often emphasizes reducing input. We conducted a mixed-methods, counterbalanced within-subjects study with 20 Chinese autistic adults who evaluated five complete XR configurations presenting the same popular-science content. Comfort differed substantially across the configurations (Friedman chi-square(4) = 46.39, p < .001, Kendall's W = .58). L3 received the lowest mean rating (2.97/5) and was tied for lowest for 16/20 participants, whereas L5 received the highest mean rating (4.43/5) and was tied for highest for 17/20. Participants described the static configurations in terms of clarity and self-pacing, L3 in terms of abruptness, simultaneous demands, insufficient warning, and limited disengagement, and L4/L5 in terms of gradual transitions, opportunities to disengage, and coordinated narrative cues. The study provides a configuration-level account of sensory comfort and identifies participant-described qualities that can inform future controlled studies of multisensory XR.

items.title: Beyond the Answer: Student-Conditioned Trace Construction for Reasoning Distillation
items.summary: A reasoning trace can accompany a correct answer without providing effective supervision for a particular student. We study how to construct traces that improve learning beyond answer-only supervision by considering both their intermediate content and their accessibility to the target learner. We introduce ReDiST, a student-conditioned trace-construction and distillation framework for evidence-rich reasoning. Starting from the student's own attempts, ReDiST revises answer-correct drafts against the supplied evidence and repairs unsuccessful drafts with additional guidance from the verified answer. A frozen student-matched reader screens and ranks original and edited candidates using answer recovery and verified-answer probability, given the question, evidence, and candidate trace. We distill the selected targets while balancing trace and final-answer supervision with an auxiliary answer loss. Construction and selection occur offline, and inference uses only the distilled student. Experiments on question-answering benchmarks show that ReDiST can improve both source-task and cross-benchmark performance over answer-only, original-trace, and the evaluated trace-selection and rewriting baselines. Across supervision recipes, performance rankings can differ between source and transfer benchmarks, highlighting the importance of evaluating trace teaching utility across distributions.

items.title: Waiting Buys Exactly Two Moments: Endogenous Identification in Prediction-Driven Allocation
items.summary: A planner with a fixed budget of preventive help must decide whom to help and when. Waiting reveals risk but removes intervention opportunities as higher-risk individuals leave first. We characterize this tradeoff under repeated noisy signals and risk-dependent attrition: in the canonical model, a length-$τ$ observation prefix identifies exactly the latent risk moments $m_j=\mathbb E[p^j]$ for $j=0,\ldots,2τ-1$, buying two new moments per additional period. These identify average next-period attrition among survivors but need not identify allocation welfare or attrition among those prioritized for treatment. Our observationally equivalent constructions establish unavoidable timing regret at any sample size for a fixed observation length, while exact certificates determine whether all compatible populations share a unique optimal date. Matched experiments separate the effects of estimation, bootstrap averaging, and regret weighting. Longer observation often resolves timing ambiguity, but the optimal date may already have passed. In our experiments, bootstrap averaging and early stopping improve decisions, while regret weighting adds no improvement in pooled mean squared regret: better statistical fit need not yield better allocation welfare. The code and artifacts are available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/waiting-buys-two-moments.

items.title: OTS-PC: OTS-based Payment Channels for the Lightning Network
items.summary: We present a new type of bidirectional payment channel based on One-Time Signatures on state sequence numbers. This new construction is simpler than the Poon-Dryja construction, but provides a number of benefits such as $O(1)$ storage per channel, minimal information leakage, and compatibility with Lightning Network routing.

items.title: Quality-of-Transmission Estimation in Quantum Networks: Compute, Simulate, or Learn?
items.summary: Future quantum networks will rely on control-plane decisions such as routing, scheduling, entanglement provisioning, purification, and memory allocation. Each decision depends on a timely and reliable estimate of the quality of the entanglement that a candidate path can deliver, with end-to-end fidelity as a central metric. Inspired by the optical-networking experience with quality-of-transmission (QoT) estimation, this article asks when a quantum controller should compute fidelity analytically, simulate it, or learn a surrogate model. The optical analogy is useful but incomplete: optical QoT estimation often predicts a scalar transmission margin, whereas quantum QoT estimation must account for probabilistic entanglement generation, random memory waiting times, decoherence, state consumption, and measurement constraints that can make fidelity a stochastic target. We propose a compute/simulate/learn framework for quantum QoT estimation and illustrate it with a simulation-based proof of concept. Our study shows that analytical composition can be sufficient in simple regimes, that simulation becomes necessary when stochastic memory effects shape the delivered fidelity distribution, and that lightweight learned surrogates can approximate simulator labels at much lower runtime cost for online control. We close with open challenges for deployment, including stochastic targets, sim-to-real transfer, data-generation cost, physics-informed learning, and generalization beyond individual paths to full network topologies.

items.title: Self-Building Labs
items.summary: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) accelerate scientific discovery by automating experimental execution and optimization. AI agents can increasingly propose new experiments, but existing SDLs can only run the procedures they were built for. Adapting them to a new experiment still takes extensive manual engineering, which makes laboratory flexibility the bottleneck for scaling discovery. We introduce the self-building laboratory (SBL), which designs, configures, and operates its own laboratory setup given a high-level scientific goal. SBL starts from whatever already exists, from an empty room to a working SDL, and builds the missing capabilities: the lab layout, its digital twin, robot skills, and experimental workflows. We demonstrate the system working across different robots and setups, scaling from a single workstation to laboratories with several robots working together. We validate SBL's end-to-end capabilities through a real-world quantum-dot synthesis experiment. By shifting the role of human researchers from manually configuring and programming device automation to specifying scientific objectives, SBL makes scientific automation more accessible, flexible, and scalable. Project website: https://self-building-labs.github.io/

items.title: ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-Matched References for Amortized Simulation-Based Model Inference
items.summary: The evidence, $\mathcal{Z} = p(x | \mathcal{M})$, of a data-generating model $\mathcal{M}$ is a powerful tool in Bayesian frameworks: it enables model inference, model misspecification tests, and goodness-of-fit assessment as an alternative to standard discrepancy statistics, e.g. $χ^2$. While versatile, the evidence is notoriously difficult to compute, even when the likelihood is available. In both likelihood-based and simulation-based inference, estimating $\mathcal{Z}$ provides an immediate solution to high-dimensional goodness-of-fit or model misspecification tests: using $\mathcal{Z}(x)$ as the test statistic induces a minimum-volume level-$α$ test. Such tests are essential to assess model fidelity, which is necessary to trust simulation-based parameter inference. Existing learned approaches largely target Bayes factors, which only measure evidence ratios. Instead, we provide accurate, fast, and amortized estimates of the absolute evidence. We present ENFR: Evidence Networks with Flow-matched References. Building on the Evidence Network framework of Jeffrey & Wandelt (2024), the proposed method first learns Bayes factors with respect to a flow-matched reference, from which the absolute evidence is recovered. We show improvement in estimation of $\mathcal{Z}$ over the flow-based baseline in all applications considered and the best performance of all density estimation methods considered in our benchmarks. We furthermore introduce and provide the proof for an architecture that jointly learns the individual evidences of a set of models $\{\mathcal{M}_i\}$. We demonstrate the performance and scaling behavior of these approaches on data from a variety of scientific applications.

items.title: Online Graph Coloring with Random Arrivals
items.summary: We study online graph coloring in the random-arrival model, where the vertices are presented in a uniformly random order. Assuming $n$ and $k$ are known in advance, we present a randomized exponential-time algorithm that colors any $k$-colorable graph on $n$ vertices with $O(k^3 \log^2 k \log^4 n)$ colors in expectation. This is the first online coloring algorithm that uses a polylogarithmic number of colors for all fixed $k \geq 3$, and is better than a known lower bound of $Ω(\log^{k-1} n)$ colors under adversarial arrivals for all fixed $k \geq 6$. In addition, assuming $n$ is known in advance, we obtain a competitive ratio of $\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})$. For comparison, it is known to be NP-hard to approximate (offline) graph coloring within a factor of $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for all fixed $\varepsilon > 0$. Therefore, our exponential-time online algorithm achieves a performance guarantee beyond the NP-hardness threshold for polynomial-time approximation algorithms.

items.title: TANGO: RNA Topology and Geometry Co-Design
items.summary: Designing RNA sequences that satisfy target tertiary-structure objectives is an important problem in RNA engineering, with broad applications in synthetic biology and therapeutics. Existing 3D RNA design methods have made substantial progress, but they largely treat the target fold as a geometry-only objective. This is incomplete for RNA, whose functional folds are specified not only by tertiary geometry but also by secondary base-pairing topology. We therefore formulate RNA inverse design as a topology-and-geometry co-design problem and propose TANGO, a multi-objective multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for this task. TANGO adopts a staged curriculum: it first learns a topology-aware policy from secondary-structure targets, then transfers this policy to tertiary-structure targets to train a general co-design model, and finally applies frontier-guided fine-tuning to refine target-specific trade-offs among secondary-structure fidelity, tertiary-structure fidelity, and sequence diversity. Experiments show that TANGO generates diverse and novel designs, improving tertiary- and secondary-structure performance by 18.3% and 52.7%, respectively, over the strongest baseline.

items.title: Learning without relearning physical symmetry: an SO(3)-equivariant convolutional network (CNN) on the sphere
items.summary: Many of the most important datasets in the physical sciences live natively on the sphere, and these data often carry no preferred position or orientation. Using methods that do not reflect this symmetry leads to far higher simulation requirements, which can be catastrophic for scientific analyses (forcing reliance on cheap, imperfect models that bias results). We present a novel spherical implementation of a gauge equivariant mesh architecture that is specifically designed for the Hierarchical Equal Area isoLatitude Pixelization (\healpix{}) of the sphere. The $\mathrm{SO}(3)$-equivariant convolution is built from steerable filters, parallel transport and spin-weighted features. The architecture supplies the exact symmetry, so the network does not spend training data learning it. The convolution operations are constructed to give provably exact equivariance, given a band-limit. Our full CNNs can achieve SO(3)-invariance error at per-cent-level and lower, which is controlled through well-understood hyperparameters. On benchmarks, our technique gives the most accurate dense gradient regression and competitive cosmic microwave background foreground removal and denoising. The improved simulation efficiency matters most in simulation-based inference (SBI), where high-fidelity simulations are expensive and neural compressors require large training sets, so a fixed budget forces analyses with less accurate simulators. In cosmology lensing SBI, our technique yields the tightest posteriors at matched simulation count. This approach is a novel method that will enable new convolutional neural network analyses, including generative and inference tasks, for processes and data on the sphere.

items.title: Automatic Tensor-level Execution of Abstract Interpreters for Neural Networks
items.summary: Developing new abstract interpretation-based DNN certifiers is difficult because their mathematical design is expressed at the neuron level, while implementations must operate at the tensor level. Existing libraries such as auto_LiRPA, IVAN, and ERAN support fixed sets of certifiers; extending them requires expertise in formal methods and tensor programming. Domain-specific languages such as ConstraintFlow let researchers specify certifiers at the neuron level, but cannot run them on real DNNs. We present Neuton, a framework that automatically translates neuron-level certifier specifications into tensor-level executables, enabling new DNN certifiers without manual tensor programming. Neuton makes three contributions. First, a stack-based intermediate representation (IR) and shape analysis infer implicit tensor operations, including broadcasts, dimension expansions, and reductions, required for correct execution. Second, domain-specific rewrite rules optimize common tensor operation sequences into more efficient equivalents. Third, gBCSR is a sparse tensor format using variable-sized, layer-aligned blocks over a non-zero default value, tailored to DNN certifier sparsity. We prove that translation preserves neuron-level semantics. We evaluate Neuton on 8 certifiers and 32 DNN benchmarks. Neuton compiles four existing certifiers and produces the first executable implementations of four others: two previously specified but never run, and two new designs. These expose precision-runtime trade-offs unavailable in existing libraries. For example, SkipPoly matches DeepPoly's precision on all 32 DNNs while running as fast or faster on half. Neuton's runtime on existing certifiers is competitive with hand-optimized libraries. Code: https://github.com/uiuc-focal-lab/constraintflow.git

items.title: CocoRNA: Collective RNA Design with Cooperative Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Designing RNA sequences that reliably fold into specific secondary structures is essential for understanding their biological functions but remains a challenging computational problem. We propose CocoRNA, a cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning framework for RNA inverse design. CocoRNA simplifies the design task by decomposing it into smaller sub-problems, each solved collaboratively by multiple agents. This approach reduces the complexity of the problem and improves the exploration of design policies. During training, a centralized critic uses global structural information to guide the agents, enabling them to jointly optimize their design strategies. As a result, CocoRNA learns high-quality RNA design policies that generalize effectively to unseen structures without additional training. Experiments on the Rfam dataset demonstrate that CocoRNA substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both success rate and design speed. Further experiments on other biological sequence design tasks highlight the effectiveness and broad potential of CocoRNA for complex design tasks.

items.title: Acceptance Is Not Speed: Length Inflation in Training-Free Lossy Speculative Decoding
items.summary: Speculative decoding typically characterizes speedup by draft tokens accepted per verification round. Lossless verification preserves the target model's output distribution and thus expected completion length, making this metric a meaningful efficiency proxy. Relaxed (lossy) verification accepts tokens that lossless verification would reject, potentially altering that distribution. We identify a length inflation phenomenon: relaxed verification lengthens completions, primarily by extending reasoning traces, largely offsetting apparent gains in accepted tokens per round. We evaluate existing training-free relaxed verification rules on twelve target-drafter pairs against lossless verification on identical prompts, measuring completion length, verifier rounds, wall-clock time, and task accuracy.
