Experiments on UltraFeedback and Argilla DPO-Mix-7k confirm that SA-DPO consistently outperforms DPO and SimPO, with a 58.5% head-to-head win-rate in downstream generation quality.

items.title: Strong Consistency and Asymptotic Normality of the Maximum Likelihood Estimator in $r$-Largest Generalized Extreme-Value Models
items.summary: We study maximum likelihood estimation in the three-parameter $r$-largest generalized extreme-value ($r$GEV) model with a fixed number $r$ of upper order statistics per block. Because the support depends on all three parameters, the classical regular theory does not apply. We show that the maximum likelihood estimator is strongly consistent on compact parameter sets contained in $k<1$, where $k=-γ$ denotes the shape parameter. For $k_0<1/2$, the range in which the model is differentiable in quadratic mean, the estimator is root-$n$ consistent, asymptotically normal and asymptotically efficient. The proof verifies the conditions of the moving-support likelihood theorem of Bücher and Segers for the ordered $r$-dimensional likelihood; the main new ingredients are a sequential modified likelihood criterion and a support-loss bound showing that the regularity threshold $k_0<1/2$ does not depend on $r$. In simulated heavy-tailed cases with only $50$ blocks, using five to seven order statistics instead of the block maximum reduces the relative bias of the 100-year return level from $6$--$13\%$ to below $5\%$.

items.title: CleanRM: Reward Modeling from Noisy Feedback with a Few Clean Feedback for RLHF
items.summary: Feedback noise is pervasive in preference data, arising from subjective human judgments, annotation mistakes, and imperfect LLM judges. Standard reward modeling trained on such feedback yields a biased estimate of the clean risk. Although classical denoising methods are directly applicable to noisy feedback learning, they generally assume a uniform noise ratio across samples. However, this assumption fails for feedback data, where noise is intrinsically sample-wise. To address this challenge, we propose CleanRM, which uses a few clean feedback to calibrate sample-wise noise ratios via optimal transport. Specifically, CleanRM aligns the joint distribution of preferences reverted from noisy feedback with that of clean feedback and then trains the reward model using a noise-corrected surrogate loss. Theoretically, we prove that the resulting objective is unbiased with respect to the clean risk. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CleanRM outperforms state-of-the-art denoising baselines and yields more effective downstream RLHF alignment.

items.title: Pathwise Shrinkage and Probabilistic Calibration of the Multiplicative Half-Cauchy Process
items.summary: We characterize the multiplicative half-Cauchy process through its log-scale random-walk representation, establishing shrinkage, expansion, and critical regimes, almost-sure summability, local rebounds, and effective dimension. We also derive a semi-analytic calibration rule linking interpretable prior probability statements to its scale parameter.

items.title: A One-Sided McDiarmid-Type Inequality for Heavy Tails via Reverse KL Tensorization
items.summary: We revisit McDiarmid's inequality, a central tool in statistical learning theory and algorithm analysis. We show that large deviations above the mean are exponentially unlikely for functions of independent random variables that are almost surely bounded above and satisfy a conditional moment assumption of order $p\in(1,2]$. When $p<2$, the result applies even when the function has infinite variance. Our proof relies on a new tensorization inequality for the Kullback--Leibler divergence, termed reverse KL tensorization, which may be of independent interest. Applications include concentration of the sample mean and median-of-means estimator, and one-sided uniform risk bounds for unbounded losses.

items.title: StochLOB: Heavy-Tailed Score Matching for Robust Limit Order Book Trend Prediction
items.summary: Score-based diffusion methods usually perturb data with Brownian Gaussian noise, corresponding to a light-tailed forward stochastic differential equation (SDE). For market time series this SDE can be a poor abstraction: limit order book (LOB) order flow is heavy-tailed, bursty, and occasionally jump-like. We study STOCHLOB, a training-only score-matching framework that changes the forward diffusion corruption law while leaving the deployed predictor deterministic. Instead of Brownian-only Gaussian corruption, the noising process uses two non-Gaussian SDE-inspired alternatives: jump-Lévy noise through a compound-Poisson variance mixture, and clipped $α$-stable noise through a positive-stable Gaussian scale mixture. These corruptions inject finite jumps and heavy-tailed residuals into training without requiring reverse-time diffusion sampling at inference. The resulting score target has a useful interpretation: its radial factor $h_t(r)$ is the posterior expected corruption precision, so large residuals are weighted according to the latent corruption scale that most plausibly generated them. On chronologically held-out Coinbase LOB data, the proposed variants remain competitive on uncorrupted BTC and altcoin test horizons and improve several realized tail-window stress diagnostics. An exploratory Feishu A-share transfer study further tests whether the probability outputs remain usable under transaction costs and trading-rule constraints. Code and configuration files are available at https://github.com/ArshiAbolghasemi/Penny.

items.title: Reliability and Preventive Maintenance for Multivariate Gamma Degradation with Shared Random Effects and Cumulative Environmental Shock Damage
items.summary: In industrial engineering, many highly reliable products have multiple performance characteristics that degrade simultaneously over time. Owing to common manufacturing factors and shared operating environments, their degradation processes are often statistically dependent. External environmental shocks may also accumulate into common damage and jointly contribute to system failure. To characterize such dependence, unit heterogeneity, and cumulative environmental damage, this study proposes a multivariate Gamma degradation model with a shared random effect and a shared environmental degradation process. Each degradation process consists of an individual Gamma process and a shared Gamma process, while the random effect captures latent heterogeneity across units and induces additional dependence. An explicit expression for system reliability is derived. For parameter estimation, an expectation maximization algorithm combined with variational inference is developed, and parametric bootstrap is used for uncertainty quantification. A preventive maintenance optimization approach is further established. Simulation studies and a coating degradation application demonstrate the effectiveness and practical applicability of the proposed methods.

items.title: Multiple testing in multi-stream sequential change detection
items.summary: Multi-stream sequential change detection involves simultaneously monitoring many data streams and raising an alarm when their distributions change. We study the multiple testing issues that arise naturally in this setting. We first point out a fundamental tension between the criteria used in change detection and multiple testing: any procedure with finite average run length (ARL) must have worst-case false discovery rate (FDR) and family-wise error rate equal to one. Given this conflict, we find a middle ground by introducing the error over patience (EOP) class of Type I error metrics, which measure error relative to expected monitoring time. To control the EOP, we propose procedures combining e-detectors, which generalize Shiryaev-Roberts and CUSUM methods, with the recent e-Benjamini-Hochberg and e-Bonferroni methods for multiple testing. Our EOP guarantees hold uniformly over changepoints and stopping times with finite expectation, allowing dependence when each e-detector remains valid using information from all streams. If finite ARL is forfeited, using e-processes instead yields ordinary FDR and per-family error control at stopping times. We also prove power and delay bounds for Gaussian changes, establish first-order minimax optimality, and compare our procedures with existing methods in numerical experiments.

items.title: ManifoldFlow: Spectrum-Learnable Stiefel Optimization via SPD Relaxation
items.summary: Orthogonal and Stiefel constraints are widely used in neural network optimization to control weight geometry, improve conditioning, and stabilize signal propagation. Yet standard Stiefel optimization imposes a hidden restriction: while learning the directions of a linear map, it fixes every singular value to one, preventing the model from learning how strongly different directions should be amplified or suppressed. We introduce ManifoldFlow, a spectrum-learnable extension of Stiefel optimization that separates directional geometry from spectral scaling through $W=QS^{1/2}$, where $Q^\top Q=I$ and $S\succ0$. Beyond simply making the spectrum trainable, ManifoldFlow uses the gradient component rejected by the Stiefel constraint as a signal for how the spectrum should change, accumulates this signal across aligned tangent spaces, and jointly updates the orthonormal basis and a bounded SPD spectrum. This construction preserves exact spectral interpretability because $W^\top W=S$, while recovering standard Stiefel optimization when $S=I$. We establish the geometry of the rejected gradient, characterize optimization over the resulting Stiefel--SPD product space, and derive how the learned spectrum affects conditioning, signal propagation, and spectral complexity. Across diverse tasks, ManifoldFlow consistently outperforms matched fixed-spectrum Stiefel baselines, with particularly strong gains in recurrent language modeling. Our code is available at https://github.com/Hik289/manifold_flow.git.

items.title: Score Mismatch and Set-Constrained Sampling in Zero-Shot Conditional Discrete Diffusion
items.summary: Discrete diffusion models have become a powerful framework for modeling complex discrete distributions across a range of applications. While theoretical convergence guarantees depend on consistency between the target and training distributions, such a case rarely holds in practice, making score mismatch a central challenge in discrete diffusion sampling. This is particularly relevant to zero-shot conditional generation, where a model trained on the unconditional distribution is directly reused at inference time to sample from a conditional target distribution. In this paper, we provide the first theoretical analysis for score-mismatched discrete diffusion models and derive a general KL divergence upper bound that clearly identifies the additional bias caused by such a mismatch. Our analysis covers partial-observation constraints, including text infilling, sentence completion, and more general coordinatewise set constraints. Specifically, we analyze the classical Conditional SEDD sampler and show that it can incur a bias term that scales with the dimension, vocabulary size, and compatibility. Based on this analysis, we propose a Randomized Hard Clamping (RHC) sampler for coordinatewise set constraints. We show that the assignment probabilities can be expressed exactly by the unconditional scores with absorbing rate. Finally, numerical and real-data experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed RHC sampler.

items.title: Supervised Learning Objectives for High-Dimensional Treatment Effects
items.summary: Predicting the effect of interventions with many possible variations, e.g., therapeutic content that affects mental health outcomes or an earnings call transcript that drives movement in share price, is useful across several domains. However, classical causal estimators tend to assume that all possible interventions are observed, which is infeasible when interventions vary widely, for instance, in the space of all text strings. We adapt a well-known approach of recasting causal inference as a learning problem to address such settings, assuming realizability of the learned function and no unobserved confounding. We show that causal error decomposes into moment-balancing errors of increasing order and exploit structure of the conditional outcome in the confounders to design objectives that directly improve causal estimation. We also show how to project the effect of a high-dimensional treatment onto coarser attributes, which allows a single model to answer several causal questions without additional attribute-specific training. We empirically evaluate our estimators in settings with high-dimensional continuous, discrete, and text treatments. Our experiments demonstrate generalization to held-out treatments, benefits of balancing higher-order moments when required, and projected causal estimates that are competitive with attribute-specific ones.

items.title: Efficient Agnostic Learning of Univariate Densities Under Local Differential Privacy
items.summary: We propose a general framework for non-interactive locally differentially private (LDP) learning of structured univariate distributions that can be approximated by piece-wise polynomials. This gives the first sample-efficient LDP learners for several distribution classes, including mixtures of log-concave distributions, such as Gaussian mixture models (GMMs). These learners also provide agnostic guarantees and are computationally efficient. We also prove a lower bound for learning GMMs under LDP, improving on the standard pure-DP packing lower bounds of Bun et al. [BKSW19]. To obtain our general learning framework, we develop an efficient non-interactive LDP algorithm for synthetic data generation over large domains, which may be of independent interest. We then use it together with a deterministic adaptation of the non-private piecewise polynomial learner of Acharya et al. [ADLS17].

items.title: On the Last-Iterate Convergence of Clipped Gradient Methods
items.summary: In stochastic (strongly) convex optimization, establishing last-iterate convergence guarantees for first-order methods has recently garnered increasing attention, as this not only deepens the theoretical understanding of these algorithms but also aligns more closely with practice. Notably, people have demonstrated that one of the most famous, simple, and popular methods, Stochastic Gradient Descent ($\mathtt{SGD}$), provably achieves last-iterate convergence. However, the existing results may have limited applicability, since they typically rely on strong conditions on the gradient noise (e.g., an exponentially decaying tail) rather than the more realistic heavy-tailed noise. Unfortunately, when faced with heavy-tailed noise, $\mathtt{SGD}$ is known to exhibit undesirable behavior or even fail to converge. To address the challenge of heavy-tailed noise, people have proposed $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$, an algorithm that combines $\mathtt{SGD}$ with a simple mechanism, gradient clipping. Although $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$ performs well in practice, its last-iterate convergence property remains highly underexplored. In this work, we prove the first optimal last-iterate rates in high probability for $\mathtt{Clipped}\text{-}\mathtt{SGD}$ under heavy-tailed noise, thereby closing a gap in the literature.

items.title: Beyond Match Results: Bayesian Mediation of Ability, Performance, and Winning in Professional Tennis
items.summary: Match results measure competitive ability, but they do not explain how ability is expressed during play. Match statistics offer a natural mediator, however performance is usually measured over the same match as the outcome: a full-match statistic uses events that help determine the winner, while a first-set statistic is earlier but rests on fewer service points and still contributes to the result. Comparing the two therefore mixes timing and precision. We develop a Bayesian mediation framework for this problem. Dynamic abilities on hard, clay, and grass courts are estimated from previous seasons only and are linked to both players' service performance, and a Bradley--Terry model relates ability and performance to the match result. A control mediator samples the first set's number of service points from the full match, separating the measurement window from the point count. In 3,820 men's matches, the hard-court mediated share rises from 0.52 with a first-set mediator to 0.95 with a full-match mediator; the point-count contrast accounts for 0.30 of this gap and the window contrast for 0.13. The pattern replicates on the women's tour. Simulations and sensitivity analyzes examine the decomposition and assumptions needed for a causal interpretation.

items.title: A Bayesian hierarchical push-forward method for cluster Randomized Controlled Trial power calculations in complex humanitarian settings
items.summary: The design and evaluation of public health interventions in humanitarian crises demand rigorous yet flexible methodological approaches. Cluster-randomized controlled trials (cRCTs) are increasingly used to generate evidence in such settings, but trial conduct is frequently complicated by displacement, resource constraints, and cluster dropout. Although Bayesian methods provide a natural framework for hierarchical modeling, probabilistic uncertainty quantification, and the integration of prior knowledge, their use in cRCT design remains limited, particularly with respect to anticipating missingness. This paper introduces a Bayesian design strategy tailored for cRCTs in complex settings, motivated by a forthcoming trial in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, that will assess a community health worker adherence intervention for cardiovascular disease and hepatitis C. Our approach incorporates prior information on cluster and individual-level dropout into power and sample size calculations via a hierarchical model and push-forward distribution framework. Through simulation studies, we evaluate the performance of the proposed method under varying levels of missingness and correlation structures. The approach is then applied to inform the design of the Bangladesh trial. We disseminate our methods via a publicly-available R Shiny app to promote accessibility and usability to investigators. By formalizing Bayesian strategies that anticipate data loss, this work provides a foundation for more robust and efficient cRCTs in humanitarian contexts; therefore, strengthening the evidence base for health interventions in resource-limited and crisis-affected populations.

items.title: GeoMix: A Bayesian Framework for Stratigraphic and Geotechnical Inference
items.summary: Accurate characterisation of subsea sediments is essential for engineering projects such as offshore wind farms, but the challenging environment and large spatial domains involved make dense geotechnical measurements impractical. Seismic traces offer a cheap, abundant complement, yet their geotechnical interpretation relies on subjective judgement, leading to biased, hard-to-validate predictions of sediment structure. To address this, we introduce GeoMix, a fully Bayesian hierarchical framework for jointly inferring geological stratigraphy and geotechnical properties from seismic and geotechnical data. GeoMix uses a Potts Markov random field to represent spatially coherent geology organised into distinct stratigraphic layers. Labels derived from seismic interpretation are linked to the latent stratigraphy through an observation model that captures elevated uncertainty near transitions between strata. Conditional on the latent stratigraphy, geotechnical properties are modelled using class-specific Gaussian processes, with scalable likelihood evaluation enabled by a grouped Vecchia approximation. Together, these components yield a unified latent-variable model capable of recovering stratigraphy, quantifying uncertainty, and predicting geotechnical properties across large three-dimensional domains. Simulation studies and an application to the IJmuiden Ver offshore wind farm show that GeoMix produces spatially coherent stratigraphic estimates and sediment predictions that are better calibrated and more accurate than existing approaches.

items.title: Acceleration and its Limits in Gaussian Variational Inference
items.summary: We study whether the classical momentum-based acceleration that improves the condition-number dependence of gradient descent from $κ$ to $\sqrtκ$ for strongly convex, smooth objectives extends to Gaussian variational inference (GVI) for strongly log-concave, log-smooth target distributions. With exact Gaussian expectations, a convex composite formulation of GVI yields the classical accelerated $\sqrtκ$ convergence rate. However, when only pointwise derivatives are available, we construct a family of strongly log-concave targets for which any randomized algorithm requires $κ^{1-o(1)}$ queries to achieve a fixed objective accuracy, even when the initial objective gap is bounded independently of $κ$. Thus curvature bounds alone cannot guarantee uniform accelerated total-query complexity. We then ask which additional structure permits acceleration and give positive examples: under a Hessian-Lipschitz assumption, variance-reduced stochastic methods yield accelerated guarantees when the Hessian variation is sufficiently small. Finally, experiments on real datasets show substantial empirical speedups from acceleration across a broad range of methods.

items.title: Stable Causal Estimation with Optimal Transport
items.summary: In observational studies, the overlap assumption, also called positivity, is frequently strained in practice. Limited overlap destabilizes widely used estimators such as inverse propensity weighting (IPW), whose variance depends on density ratios that explode as propensity scores approach zero or one. To address this challenge, we propose the Stable Transport Estimator (STE), an optimal transport-based approach for estimating average causal effects when overlap holds but strict overlap fails. Unlike IPW, the variance of STE contains no density-ratio factor; it is governed by the transport map itself and stays finite under bounded moments, even when density ratios diverge. By replacing reweighting with a geometry-aware transport map, STE constructs stable counterfactual comparisons without requiring density estimation or propensity score modeling. STE further extends to settings where the overlap condition is violated: when covariate supports overlap only partially, a linear interpolation transport map enables principled extrapolation with explicit bias-variance trade-offs. We establish consistency, asymptotic normality, and a variance characterization that makes explicit the contribution of the estimated transport map to the asymptotic variance. Across synthetic and real datasets, STE demonstrates improved robustness, reduced bias, and markedly more stable variance compared to existing estimators.

items.title: Failure Is the Mother of Success: Recovering Supervision with Grounding Hindsight
items.summary: When every rollout for a problem fails, GRPO receives neither a successful exemplar nor a nonzero group-relative advantage, so it learns nothing from exactly the problems it most needs to learn. The failed reasoning can nevertheless suggest what to try next. We present Replay-Selected Hindsight Distillation (RSHD), which turns failed attempts into an additional, tested source of supervision during GRPO training. The policy writes a corrective note about each failed attempt without seeing a reference answer or solution, then re-solves the problem with the note in context. A note is admitted only if its replays succeed more often than the original group did, after screening for notes that state the answer, and an admitted replay is distilled into the plain-prompt policy. Because admission is decided by fresh successes rather than by the failed rollout itself, the procedure can recover supervision from groups in which every attempt failed, and it applies equally to failures in mixed groups. Only the policy is trained, the only judge is the outcome verifier, and deployment requires no notes or extra inference. Across model families and sizes and two training domains, RSHD consistently improves over GRPO on in-domain benchmarks, and the gains carry over to out-of-domain evaluation sets.

items.title: Halve-Then-Greedy: Adaptive Sampling for Posterior Success with Near-Optimal Instance Dependence
items.summary: We study fixed-budget adaptive experimentation aimed at maximizing the probability of obtaining sufficient posterior evidence that a recommended design's mean performance exceeds a target. Unlike best-arm identification, this objective does not require finding the best design. For Gaussian bandits with a Gaussian prior, we propose \emph{Halve-Then-Greedy} (HTG), which combines a large initial balanced allocation, successive halving, and posterior-greedy sampling. We prove instance-dependent, finite-budget exponential bounds on posterior-failure probability that capture both separation from unfavorable arms and the presence of multiple favorable arms. On one-positive-arm families, we establish an asymptotic sample-complexity lower bound that HTG matches up to a logarithmic factor. We further analyze uniform sampling and sequential halving, revealing regimes where they require more samples than HTG by linear and logarithmic factors, respectively. Simulations illustrate HTG's sample-efficiency advantages and their dependence on instance structure.

items.title: PAC-Causal Learnability: From Identification to Finite-Sample Guarantees
items.summary: Causal identification asks whether a causal target can be recovered from the observational distribution in an idealized infinite-data setting. In practice, only finite samples are available, and identifiability alone does not determine how much data are needed for reliable estimation. We introduce Probably Approximately Correct Causal (PACC) learnability, which formalizes uniform accuracy-confidence guarantees over a causal model class. From a PAC-learning perspective, we ask how many samples are sufficient to estimate a causal target to accuracy $ε$ with probability at least $1-δ$. We show that PACC sample complexity is shaped by three recurring factors: causal identification strength, target complexity, and nuisance complexity, and derive a general sufficient bound linking them to finite-sample causal learning. We illustrate the framework through self-controlled case series, instrumental variables, and propensity-score-based estimation, showing how distinct causal methods can be analyzed within a common framework.

items.title: What is the price of approximation? The saddlepoint approximation to a likelihood function
items.summary: The saddlepoint approximation to the likelihood, and its corresponding maximum likelihood estimate (MLE), offer an alternative estimation method when the true likelihood is intractable or computationally expensive. However, maximizing this approximated likelihood instead of the true likelihood inevitably comes at a price: a discrepancy between the MLE derived from the saddlepoint approximation and the true MLE. In previous studies, the size of this discrepancy has been investigated via simulation, or by engaging with the true likelihood despite its computational difficulties. Here, we introduce an explicit and computable approximation formula for the discrepancy, through which the adequacy of the saddlepoint-based MLE can be directly assessed. We present examples demonstrating the accuracy of this formula in specific cases where the true likelihood can be calculated. Additionally, we present asymptotic results that capture the behaviour of the discrepancy in a suitable limiting framework.

items.title: A Model Ensemble-Based Post-Processing Framework for Fairness-Aware Prediction
items.summary: Striking an optimal balance between predictive performance and fairness continues to be a fundamental challenge in machine learning. In this work, we propose a post-processing framework that facilitates fairness-aware prediction by leveraging model ensembling. Designed to operate independently of any specific model internals, our approach is widely applicable across various learning tasks, model architectures, and fairness definitions. Through extensive experiments spanning classification, regression, and survival analysis, we demonstrate that the framework effectively enhances fairness while maintaining, or only minimally affecting, predictive accuracy.

items.title: Two-Stage Score Estimation for Group-Specific Diffusion Models
items.summary: Generative modeling across related distributions raises a question: how can shared structure support accurate generation for a target distribution with limited observations? We develop a statistical framework for diffusion transfer that analyzes a shared pooled score together with a target-specific offset. Under Besov regularity of the pooled density and a stable hierarchical composition model for the offset, we derive convergence rates that separate the costs of learning these components and identify when a simpler offset yields a faster risk-bound rate than separate fitting. Under suitable boundary and regularity assumptions, we prove that the offset remains bounded and jointly regular as diffusion time approaches zero. These results allow the lower time cutoff to vanish polynomially and provide total-variation guarantees for diffusion models as density estimators. Synthetic simulations and image benchmarks provide a proof of concept for the framework.

items.title: Nonconvex Composite Functional Constraints via First-Order Augmented Lagrangian Methods under Local Regularity
items.summary: We study nonasymptotic convergence of primal-dual methods for a class of nonconvex constrained optimization problems under local multiplier regularity. Both the objective and functional inequality constraints are compositions of convex Lipschitz outer functions with smooth nonlinear mappings. Unlike existing analyses requiring regularity globally or along the entire iterate sequence, we impose multiplier regularity only near the feasible set. Using an auxiliary minimax problem with a compact dual set, we derive Lyapunov estimates that identify nearly feasible iterates under feasible initialization and a sufficiently large penalty, without assuming multiplier boundedness. Local regularity then bounds the associated multipliers and makes dual truncation inactive, yielding approximate KKT certificates for the original problem. The smoothed prox-linear augmented Lagrangian method with dual regularization yields an $O(K^{-1/3})$ KKT residual rate. Without regularization, piecewise linear outer functions and additional local structural assumptions yield a local dual error bound and the sharper $O(K^{-1/2})$ rate.

items.title: Are continuous models better than areal models for spatial disease mapping with a large number of small areas?
items.summary: Classical methods for analysing areal mortality data typically rely on Poisson mixed models, which account for spatial and unstructured variability through prior distributions such as the BYM2 prior. This paper investigates alternative modeling approaches for settings involving a large number of small areas. Specifically, we explore the Stochastic Partial Differential Equation (SPDE) approach for continuous risk surfaces, examining an existing model from the literature alongside a proposed modification that incorporates an unstructured random effect. Finally, we evaluate the performance of both hierarchical mixed Poisson models and SPDE-based frameworks through a comprehensive simulation study across various spatial configurations and aggregation levels. Furthermore, we apply these approaches to the analysis of lung cancer mortality among men and women across Spanish municipalities during the period 2009--2022.

items.title: Near-Exponential Convergence Rates for kNN Classification based on Boltzmann Margin
items.summary: Convergence-rate analysis for classifiers is often conducted under either Tsybakov margin or Massart margin. The former is a relatively weak condition that typically yields polynomial rates, while the latter is substantially stronger but can guarantee exponential rates. In this paper, we introduce a new condition, called Boltzmann margin, that bridges the gap between these two regimes. It is weaker than Massart margin, generally stronger than Tsybakov margin, and can imply many of their properties under suitable conditions. We apply Boltzmann margin to the analysis of kNN classifiers and establish the first near-exponential convergence rates for kNN classification. We also present extensions of the main results and provide numerical evidence supporting the main theoretical implications.

items.title: Sign Betting for Misspecified Regression: Variance Adaptivity and Optimal Approximation
items.summary: We study bounded regression under model misspecification, evaluating a function $f$ by its $L_1(P_X)$ distance to the conditional mean $η(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$, rather than the standard $L_2(P_X)$. This $L_1$ metric is natural for downstream decision problems such as bandits and reinforcement learning. We analyze the min--max estimator of Baraud & Maillard (2025), which we call \emph{sign-betting regression}. Our main results show that sign-betting regression achieves high-probability $L_1$ oracle inequalities under misspecification. Under realizability, our bound adapts to the average conditional variance and recovers the variance-adaptive rate of Li et al. (2026). We further characterize the optimal universal approximation factor for proper learning by showing that sign betting achieves factor 3, while no proper learner can satisfy a distribution-free, high-probability $L_1$ oracle inequality with a universal approximation factor strictly below 3. We extend the upper-bound analysis beyond finite classes and complement the theory with experiments in synthetic and real-world model-selection tasks.

items.title: Formal Bayesian Transfer Learning via the Total Risk Prior
items.summary: Existing methods for transfer learning struggle to deal with situations where the source datasets are limited and not guaranteed to be well-aligned with the target dataset. A typical strategy is to use the empirical loss minimizer on the source data as a prior mean for the target parameters. We propose using a risk minimizer conditional on source parameters instead. This allows us to construct a joint posterior for all parameters from the source and target datasets. As a consequence, we benefit from full Bayesian uncertainty quantification and can perform model averaging via Gibbs sampling over indicator variables governing the inclusion of each source dataset. We show how a particular instantiation of our prior leads to a Bayesian Lasso in a transformed coordinate system and describe connections between the Maximum a Posteriori estimate associated with our approach and the Trans-Lasso method. We find that the MAP estimator MSE-dominates the Trans-Lasso in the normal means setting when there is no regularization on the source datasets. Finally, we perform numerical experiments finding that our approach provides superior predictive performance relative to frequentist and Bayesian baselines on a genetics application, particularly when the source data are limited.

items.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent: A Nonlinear Time Series Perspective
items.summary: This paper investigates the statistical behavior of Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) with constant step size under the framework of iterated random functions. Compared to previous studies establishing the convergence of SGD in probability measure, e.g., Wasserstein distance, our approach directly provides the convergence in Euclidean distance by showing the Geometric Moment Contraction (GMC) of SGD. This new convergence can address the non-stationarity of SGD due to fixed initial points and can provide a more refined asymptotic analysis of SGD. Specifically, we prove quenched central limit theorem, invariance principle and $α$-stable convergence for averaged SGD (ASGD) regardless of initialization. Furthermore, we provide a novel perspective to understand the impact of step sizes in SGD by studying its derivative with respect to the step size. The existence of stationary solutions for the derivative processes is shown, enabling the use of interpolation to recover the full-trajectory of SGD. Subsequently, we utilize multiple step sizes and show an enhanced Richardson-Romberg extrapolation with improved bias representation, which brings ASGD estimates closer to the global optimum. Finally, we propose a new online inference method and a bias-reduced variant for the extrapolated ASGD. Empirical confidence intervals are constructed and the coverage probabilities approach the nominal level as $n$ grows.

items.title: Flexible Doubly Robust Proximal Causal Inference for Censored Outcomes
items.summary: Estimating causal effects on right-censored time-to-event outcomes is challenging under unmeasured confounding. Proximal causal inference addresses unmeasured confounding through proxy variables, but existing proximal survival methods rely largely on restrictive parametric bridge models. We introduce Proximal Survival Bridge learning (PSB), a flexible doubly robust proximal framework for censored outcomes. Building on existing proximal identification of treatment-specific survival curves, the framework yields outcome-bridge (OB), treatment-bridge (TB), and doubly robust (DR) estimators, with two flexible bridge learners: PSB-K, a kernel estimator with a low-rank time decomposition, and PSB-N, a neural estimator trained by a projected maximum-moment-restriction loss. Unlike existing flexible proximal learners for scalar outcomes, PSB directly handles censoring and survival-curve targets. On a standard SEM benchmark, a proximal semi-synthetic ACTG study, and the real-world Framingham study, PSB-K performs strongest on SEM and ACTG, whereas PSB-N is the most stable on Framingham. Additional results with modern causal survival baselines, weakened or invalid proxies, and heavier censoring assess robustness across challenging settings.

items.title: A Mixture-of-Experts Framework for Multi-Stream Quickest Change Detection
items.summary: A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) framework is proposed for quickest change detection (QCD) where there are multiple experts, and each expert produces a sequence of statistics for change detection. A change is declared when a weighted sum of these statistics crosses a threshold. This framework is then applied to the problem of multi-stream QCD to obtain a family of powerful algorithms that outperform the best known algorithms in the literature. In the multi-stream QCD problem, a decision-maker observes multiple streams of observations. At the change point, the distribution of an unknown subset of the streams changes. The optimal algorithm based on a generalized likelihood ratio is computationally expensive. One of the most computationally and performance-efficient algorithms in the literature is the rank-weighted sum (RWS) scheme based on Shiryaev-Roberts statistics. It is shown in the paper that the MoE-based QCD algorithm for multi-stream data outperforms the RWS scheme. This is demonstrated through simulation results on real-valued Gaussian mean shift data and high-dimensional data from Gaussian--Bernoulli Restricted Boltzmann Machines (GB-RBMs).

items.title: A Greedy PDE Router for Blending Neural Operators and Classical Methods
items.summary: When solving PDEs, classical numerical solvers are often computationally expensive, while machine learning methods can suffer from spectral bias, failing to capture high-frequency components. Designing an optimal hybrid iterative solver--where, at each iteration, a solver is selected from an ensemble of solvers to leverage their complementary strengths--poses a challenging combinatorial problem. While greedy selection is desirable for its constant-factor approximation guarantee to the optimal solution under Lipschitz assumptions, it requires knowledge of the true error at each step, which is unavailable in practice. We address this by proposing an approximate greedy router that efficiently mimics a greedy approach to solver selection. Empirical results on the Poisson, convection-diffusion, and anisotropic diffusion equations show that our method consistently reduces time-to-solution relative to single-solver baselines and existing hybrid approaches such as HINTS.

items.title: A Distribution-to-Distribution Neural Probabilistic Forecasting Framework for Dynamical Systems
items.summary: Probabilistic forecasts provide a principled representation of forecast uncertainty through predictive distributions. Directly propagating predictive distributions with conventional physical models requires solving distributional evolution equations, a task well-known to be computationally prohibitive for high-dimensional nonlinear systems. Consequently, multi-step predictive distributions are commonly approximated using ensembles or sampled trajectories. A novel distribution-to-distribution (D2D) neural probabilistic forecasting framework is proposed with compatible distributional encoding and decoding interfaces around a replaceable neural forecasting module. Kernel mean embeddings represent input distributions, while mixture density networks parameterise outputs, enabling recursive multi-step forecasting in distributional form. The framework is demonstrated on the Lorenz63 system. Results show that the D2D model captures nontrivial distributional evolution, produces skillful probabilistic forecasts without explicit ensemble simulation, and remains competitive with a naively initialised perfect-model benchmark. This provides proof-of-concept evidence that predictive distributions can be recursively propagated through a neural forecasting model and evaluated in terms of probabilistic forecast performance.

items.title: Clinically Interpretable Biological Age Estimation Using CatBoost and SHAP with Continuous and Categorical Features from NHANES
items.summary: Biological age (BA) captures inter-individual variation in physiological aging beyond chronological age (CA). Although machine-learning models have advanced BA estimation, many rely primarily on continuous laboratory biomarkers, and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) dependence plots are typically interpreted visually. We developed a clinically interpretable machine-learning framework for BA estimation using heterogeneous clinical data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES 2011-March 2020, N = 24,983 adults aged >= 18). A CatBoost regression model incorporated 44 demographic, laboratory, physical examination, and lifestyle predictors to estimate CA, defining model-estimated age as BA. SHAP provided multi-level interpretability. Crucially, building on standard visual inspection, we implemented a prespecified automated procedure directly on SHAP dependence plots to quantify feature-value ranges associated with lowest and highest BA contributions, corresponding adjustment magnitudes, and zero-crossing thresholds. Model-estimated BA strongly correlated with CA in held-out testing data (Pearson r = 0.798, P < 0.001). Population-level SHAP identified blood urea nitrogen, serum glucose, vigorous recreational activity, red cell distribution width, and alanine aminotransferase among the leading predictors, with three categorical variables ranking among the top 25. Automated quantitative SHAP analysis mapped predictor-specific ranges, effect sizes, and inflection points, while waterfall plots enabled individual explanations. By extending qualitative visual interpretation to reproducible quantitative metrics across heterogeneous clinical data, this framework enhances transparency and provides a scalable methodological foundation for biological aging research and precision health.

items.title: Calibrated Bayesian inference for overall and subgroup-specific causal effects in stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trials
items.summary: Stepped-wedge cluster-randomized trials (SW-CRTs) randomly assign clusters to sequences that determine when each cluster switches from control to intervention. Conventional Bayesian analyses of SW-CRTs report treatment effect coefficients from a working outcome model, but under model misspecification or informative cluster-period sizes, such coefficients can lack a clear causal interpretation. In this work, we develop Bayesian methods targeting weighted average treatment effect estimands in SW-CRTs, including novel subgroup-specific causal estimands defined by baseline characteristics. We compare model-based g-computation with model-robust standardization, implementing both with linear mixed models and mixed-effects Bayesian additive regression trees as working outcome models, and propose a calibrated variance estimator that augments posterior parameter uncertainty with cluster-level resampling to better capture sampling variability. In simulations with outcome model misspecification and informative cluster-period sizes, model-robust standardization with calibrated inference exhibits negligible bias and near-nominal frequentist coverage for overall and subgroup-specific causal effects, whereas g-computation and uncalibrated intervals become insufficient. We illustrate the proposed methods with a reanalysis of the Trauma Survivors Outcomes and Support trial.

items.title: Complete or Sparse: A Tale of Two Identifiabilities
items.summary: Understanding when neural networks learn interpretable representations is central to mechanistic interpretability. We study this through identifiability: when can supervised learning recover the true latent variables underlying the data? We introduce two data generating processes distinguished by their causal direction where either labels cause latents (generative) or latents cause labels (discriminative). When the representation has at least as many dimensions as the latent space, we prove that the optimal encoders are linear in the latents. Conversely, when dimensions are insufficient, identifiability generically fails and encoders become nonlinear. We then show that additional constraints yield recovery of individual latent variables, not just linear mixtures. In the generative setting, non-negative activations and energy efficiency force each neuron to encode exactly one latent, providing a precise account of selective grandmother cell-like responses. In the discriminative setting, when latents are sparse and the true measurement matrix satisfies the spark condition, the learned encoder inherits compressed sensing structure, enabling sparse dictionary learning to perfectly recover individual latents. This constitutes, to our knowledge, the first identifiability result for undercomplete nonlinear independent component analysis. Our framework unifies nonlinear ICA, compressed sensing, and neural network interpretability, delineating exactly when representations transition from nonlinear distortions to linear representations and, under additional constraints or steps, to clean, axis-aligned codes. Theoretical predictions are validated on synthetic benchmarks and on activations drawn from vision models, large language models, and macaque inferotemporal cortex.

items.title: Improving ecological inference and uncertainty quantification from camera trap data through the fusion of AI confidences and manual annotations
items.summary: Camera traps have become an important tool in ecological research, enabling large-scale, noninvasive monitoring of wildlife populations and behavior. By automatically recording animals as they pass within view, these devices generate massive image datasets with minimal field effort. This data richness introduces a new bottleneck when translating the images into usable information due to time and effort required for human annotation. Artificial intelligence (AI) has recently been integrated into the workflow to improve efficiency. However, the data procured from AI approaches are of a different nature, necessitating new statistical methods. We develop a new Bayesian hierarchical data-fusion model that combines the strengths of human annotations and AI predictions. The benefits of our approach are an ability to provide uncertainty quantification as well as improved inference and predictive power, which we demonstrate through simulation. We apply our model to an AI analysis of the body condition of white-tailed deer (Odocoileus virginianus) from camera trap images from North Carolina to study the relationship between health and their environment. Our analysis derived novel ecological inference compared to a more traditional approach using the same data. We find that bucks in rut have higher (healthier) body condition than other deer and that green, open habitats are correlated with high body condition.

items.title: Challenges and Opportunities in Statistical Analyses and Designs for Neuroscience Clinical Trials
items.summary: Drug development is a complex, costly, and high-risk process, with neuroscience representing one of the most challenging therapeutic areas due to the complexity of neurodegenerative and neuropsychiatric disorders. Neuroscience clinical trials face unique barriers, making the adoption of innovative statistical methods in study design, execution, and analysis especially critical for improving clarity, feasibility, efficiency, and validity in the drug development process. The ASA Biopharmaceutical Section Neuroscience Scientific Working Group (SWG) was formed to advance statistical research and address these distinct challenges. This landscape paper provides an overview of key challenges and opportunities in statistical methods and trial designs for neuroscience, offering insights to guide future research and practice in this evolving field.

items.title: Optimal Condition for Initialization Variance in Deep Neural Networks: An SGD Dynamics Perspective
items.summary: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD), one of the most fundamental optimization algorithms in machine learning (ML), can be recast through a continuous-time approximation as a Fokker-Planck equation for Langevin dynamics, a viewpoint that has motivated many theoretical studies. Within this framework, we study the relationship between the quasi-stationary distribution derived from this equation and the initial distribution through the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. As the quasi-steady-state distribution depends on the expected cost function, the KL divergence eventually reveals the connection between the expected cost function and the initialization distribution. By applying this to deep neural network models (DNNs), we can express the bounds of the expected loss function explicitly in terms of the initialization parameters. Then, by minimizing this bound, we obtain an optimal condition of the initialization variance in the Gaussian case. This result provides a concrete mathematical criterion, rather than a heuristic approach, to select the scale of weight initialization in DNNs. In addition, we experimentally confirm our theoretical results by using the classical SGD to train fully connected neural networks on the MNIST and Fashion-MNIST datasets. The result shows that if the variance of the initialization distribution satisfies our theoretical optimal condition, then the corresponding DNN model always achieves lower final training loss and higher test accuracy than the conventional He-normal initialization. Our work thus supplies a mathematically grounded indicator that guides the choice of initialization variance and clarifies its physical meaning of the dynamics of parameters in DNNs.

items.title: Computational and Statistical Hardness of Calibration Distance
items.summary: The distance from calibration, introduced by Błasiok, Gopalan, Hu, and Nakkiran (STOC 2023), has recently emerged as a central measure of miscalibration for probabilistic predictors. We study the fundamental problems of computing and estimating this quantity, given either an exact description of the data distribution or only sample access to it. We give an efficient algorithm that exactly computes the calibration distance when the distribution has a uniform marginal and noiseless labels, which improves the $O(1/\sqrt{|\mathcal{X}|})$ additive approximation of Qiao and Zheng (COLT 2024) for this special case. Perhaps surprisingly, the problem becomes $\mathsf{NP}$-hard when either of the two assumptions is removed. We extend our algorithm to a polynomial-time approximation scheme for the general case. For the estimation problem, we show that $Θ(1/ε^3)$ samples are sufficient and necessary for the empirical calibration distance to be upper bounded by the true distance plus $ε$. In contrast, a polynomial dependence on the domain size -- incurred by the learning-based baseline -- is unavoidable for two-sided estimation. Our positive results are based on simple sparsifications of both the distribution and the target predictor, which significantly reduce the search space for computation and lead to stronger concentration for the estimation problem. To prove the hardness results, we introduce new techniques for certifying lower bounds on the calibration distance -- a problem that is hard in general due to its $\textsf{co-NP}$-completeness.

items.title: A Geometric Framework for the Bayesian Estimation of Joint Environmental Extremes
items.summary: Multivariate extreme events tend to have broader impacts on society compared to individual extremes. Flexible and accurate modeling of multivariate extremes is therefore crucial for many practical applications, including risk assessments and mitigation projects. In this work, we introduce a Bayesian modeling framework for bivariate extremes. Our approach utilizes the geometric extremes framework, for which data are decomposed into angular and radial components. The angular distribution is estimated using periodic M-splines, resulting in a natural circular density, while the radial distribution, conditional on the angles, is approximated using Bezier splines. The radial distribution also provides a means of estimating the limit set, the limiting shape of scaled sample clouds that encodes information pertaining to extremal dependence. Our Bayesian approach offers advantages over competing methods, particularly for uncertainty quantification and interpretation. Furthermore, our framework guarantees theoretical properties of limit sets, ensuring validity for inference. Notably, our model can be used to approximate extreme probabilities associated with failure sets in the joint tail, which are useful across many applications. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through numerical experiments and a case study on fire weather in Louisiana, USA, with diagnostics for the latter indicating strong model performance.

items.title: Precise Asymptotics for Dense High-Dimensional Huber Regression under Heteroscedasticity
items.summary: We study Huber regression in a heteroscedastic linear model in the proportional regime $n/p \to δ\in (1, \infty)$. Our main result is an exact characterization of the asymptotic empirical distribution of the Huber estimator. This characterization is in terms of three scalar parameters which determine the first-order centre and the asymptotic variance of the Huber estimator. The result shows that with heteroscedastic noise, the first-order centre may contain an additional component along the variance index coefficient. We derive the displacement coefficients that determine this centre, as well as the exact asymptotic variance. The analysis uses the matrix approximate message passing (AMP) framework to jointly track the regression and variance index coefficients, extending the existing framework for homoscedastic M-estimators. We illustrate the implications of this characterization by constructing a test for centre displacement and examining its empirical size and power through simulations.

items.title: Simplicity Above Elegance: Another Look at the Asymptotically Correct Standardization of Snijders
items.summary: Person-fit statistics are widely used to detect aberrant response patterns in educational and psychological measurement. Snijders (2001) suggested an asymptotically correct standardization for a broad class of such statistics. This paper presents an alternative derivation of this standardization. The derivation yields several advantages including a simpler formula and simpler description of several person-fit statistics including the lz* statistic (van Krimpen-Stoop & Meijer, 1999) and a theoretical explanation of simulation findings reported by Snijders (2001) and van Krimpen-Stoop and Meijer (1999), among others.

items.title: LASER: Latent Space Adjoint Matching for Support-Constrained Entropy-Regularized Offline RL
items.summary: While offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables policy optimization from static datasets without costly online interaction, it remains bottlenecked by the risk of executing out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. Recent approaches mitigate this by learning a behavior-cloning policy through flow matching and then performing RL within its constrained latent space. However, naively optimizing the latent policy can easily cause the policy to collapse into a brittle mode or exploit sharp artifacts of the learned critic. In this work, we find that entropy regularization is essential in latent-space RL for addressing these challenges. We introduce LASER, a novel offline RL algorithm that applies latent-space adjoint matching to achieve entropy-regularized latent-space RL with expressive flow policies while avoiding backpropagation through time. Through comprehensive experiments on 40 challenging OGBench tasks with varying dataset qualities, we show that LASER achieves state-of-the-art performance. Notably, LASER uses fixed method-specific hyperparameters across all tasks and outperforms the evaluated baselines, including those with task- and dataset-specific tuning, which highlights the robust applicability of LASER. Project website: https://mit-realm.github.io/laser/.

items.title: Selection-Safe Conformal Early Exit: Distribution-Free Coverage under Adaptive Depth
items.summary: Calibrating a conformal prediction set at each early exit does not preserve coverage once a data-dependent exit is selected. We construct one terminal path score from prefix maxima, calibrate a single split-conformal quantile, and return nested prefix sets that all contain the valid terminal set. The guarantee is selection-safe without an alpha/L correction and holds simultaneously for every post-calibration label-free stopping policy that preserves terminal-set containment. We also bound the efficiency cost of the path maximum by the empirical tail of the early-over-terminal score excess. Across eight encoder task-backbone cells, pathwise selection attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814 for naive layerwise selection, with average set size 1.41 and latency fraction 0.71. On CIFAR-100 with a 24-exit ViT-L/16 (n_cal=500), first-eligible stopping at budget b=4 attains coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57, and the same calibration supports deployment-time budget changes without refitting. In a joint exit-count/calibration-size sweep at n=100, pathwise set size moves only from 3.02 to 3.11 as exits increase from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni degenerates to the full label space for 12 or more exits. Paired comparison against MinSE valid selection at (n,L)=(100,24) gives a set-size difference of 0.80 [0.47, 1.13]. Full-vocabulary decoder experiments remain a negative boundary, with sets of 7,162-9,620 tokens. Pathwise calibration is most useful when candidate exits are many relative to calibration size, when budgets change after calibration, and when shallow heads return actionable sets.

items.title: The Reach of Treatment Effects: Randomization Inference for Zero-Effect Regions
items.summary: A treatment may affect some individuals while leaving others unaffected. We study the reach of treatment effects by asking how large an unaffected covariate region could be. We develop efficient local randomization tests over nearest-neighbour regions to construct a finite-sample valid upper confidence bound for the size of the largest zero-effect region. A small bound provides evidence that treatment effects extend broadly across covariate values by ruling out large zero-effect regions. Under a general outcome model, we characterize how the size of the bound depends on the number of affected units, the size of their treatment effects, and the geometry of the true zero-effect set. We show that, when region size is measured as a sample fraction, the excess of the upper confidence bound over the true size decreases to zero at a minimax optimal rate up to a logarithmic factor. Numerical simulations assess the coverage, power and computational efficiency of our method. Applications to voter-turnout, HIV clinical-trial, and AI-assisted writing data illustrate how our method rules out large zero-effect regions across the covariates of interest.

items.title: What Does a Discrete Diffusion Model Learn? One Reverse Process in Three Coordinates
items.summary: What does a discrete diffusion model actually learn? The literature trains denoisers, bridge plug-ins, and concrete scores, each deriving its own ELBO objective under different conventions. This fragmentation makes the object being learned unclear and ELBO values difficult to interpret and compare. All three methods learn the same object in different coordinates: the exact time-reversal of the noising process. We first prove the Oracle Distance identity: for any noising process, the negative ELBO is not just a bound on the likelihood; it equals the data entropy plus the path KL divergence from the reversed noising process to the learned one. Next, for token-factorizing noise, we show that denoiser, bridge plug-in, and concrete score are three coordinates of this reverse process, derive exact conversions between them, and identify the probability distribution learned by each. In particular, contrary to its standard interpretation, the bridge plug-in learns not a denoiser but the cavity distribution: the clean token given the noisy sequence excluding its own position. We confirm the theory by training all three coordinates with masked, uniform, and GIDD kernels on OpenWebText under a shared recipe, and by training uniform-diffusion solvers on four logic tasks. The learned coordinates agree after conversion, while confusing the cavity with the denoiser can severely degrade sampling quality. Together with exact boundary-term formulas, closed-form NELBO calibrations at initialization, and a clock interpretation of time schedules, these results provide a conceptual framework and a mechanical recipe for deriving, implementing, and comparing discrete diffusion processes.

items.title: The Zero Pattern of a Design Matrix Drives Multiple Descent in Over-parameterized Regression
items.summary: Over-parameterized linear regression has been widely studied over the last decade. However, most existing works assume that the covariates are independent and that their covariance matrices are non-degenerate. In this paper, we relax both assumptions and derive deterministic equivalents for the prediction risk in a vanishing-ridge regime. We show that degeneracy of the covariance matrices and dependence can lead to multiple descent, and characterize where the corresponding peaks can occur. Our proofs use a novel graph representation of the variance profile. We show that maximum matchings and the Dulmage--Mendelsohn decomposition of the associated bipartite graph identify the configurations at which the variance becomes singular.

items.title: Bootstrap inference in factor-augmented regressions with weak factors
items.summary: In this paper, we develop bootstrap methods for factor-augmented regressions with potentially weak common components, allowing signal eigenvalues to diverge at heterogeneous rates $N^{α_k}$, where $0<α_k\leq1$, $k=1,\ldots,r$. The regression estimator targets a rotation of the latent parameter vector that may be data dependent, while factor estimation can induce asymptotic bias. The proposed procedure directly constructs the rotation-specific target in the bootstrap world, avoiding the additional randomness induced by existing bootstrap methods. Bootstrap distributional validity is established for two data-dependent targets and a signal-dependent population target, where studentization provides asymptotically pivotal statistics for both analytical and bootstrap bias-corrected estimators. The analysis also distinguishes distributional approximation relative to a data-dependent target from inference on fixed population restrictions and introduces a bootstrap diagnostic for rotation uncertainty (RU) when signal eigenvalues are close. Monte Carlo experiments show improved bias correction, gains from bootstrap distributional approximation, and demonstrate that inference distortions from small signal eigengaps dissipate quickly with $T$ for fixed targets, in contrast to the persistent distortions under random rotations. An application to excess bond return predictability illustrates the practical importance of bootstrap distributional approximation and rotation uncertainty for inference on individual factor coefficients.

items.title: The Physics Is the Network: Fast, Training-Free Neural Emulation
items.summary: Neural emulation need not require learning a substitute for known physics. We investigate PolyNets that couple a continuous-time neural representation of polynomial dynamics with a simple recurrent network for discrete-time integration. When the governing coefficients are known, the resulting tensor graph requires no training and preserves the prescribed numerical scheme while enabling efficient hardware execution and parallel simulation. Using the one-dimensional Korteweg-de Vries equation, we compare PolyNet with CPU and GPU finite-difference Runge-Kutta solvers and three trained neural models: a state-map emulator, a physics-informed predictor, and a learned-tendency integrator. Analytical soliton solutions provide a reference for amplitude and phase errors across grid resolutions, 10^6 dispersively scaled time steps, ensembles of up to 10^4 trajectories, and varying initial amplitudes. PolyNet achieves accuracy comparable to the numerical solvers, including at amplitudes outside the learned models' training conditions. It combines this fidelity with high GPU throughput, approximately constant over the tested resolution range, and favorable ensemble scaling.

items.title: On Complexity of Gaussian Sampling
items.summary: We study the number of exact matrix-vector queries needed to sample a centered $d$-dimensional Gaussian with condition number at most $κ$ to total variation error $\varepsilon$. The best known algorithm uses $O(\min\{d,\sqrtκ\log(\frac{d}{\varepsilon})\})$ queries, while the known lower bounds do not grow as $\varepsilon\to0$ and match this bound only for $κ\le d^{1/5-δ}$ at constant accuracy. We introduce a construction based on a hidden determinant sign and prove a lower bound of $Ω\!\left(\min\left\{d,\sqrtκ\log\left(1+\frac{d}{\sqrtκ\,\varepsilon}\right)\right\}\right)$ uniformly for all $d\ge1$, $κ\ge4$, and $0<\varepsilon\le\tfrac{1}{16}$. This bound matches the known upper bound up to constant factors whenever $κ\le d^{2-δ}$ for fixed $δ\in(0,2)$, or $\varepsilon\le d^{-c}$ for fixed $c>0$. We also extend a recent fixed-spectrum construction with a hidden eigenbasis from $κ=2$ to $2\leκ\le d^{1-δ}$, for any fixed $δ\in(0,1)$. This gives an $Ω_δ(\sqrtκ\log d)$ lower bound at constant accuracy that holds even when the spectrum of the precision matrix is known to the algorithm.

items.title: Sharp Statistical Thresholds for Attributed Gaussian Graph Matching
items.summary: We investigate the problem of matching networks where both edge weights and node features are correlated following a specific node correspondence. While prior work has established sharp thresholds for matching either graphs or features individually, the joint setting has been significantly less explored. In this study, we derive precise information-theoretic thresholds for exact recovery, almost-exact recovery, and partial recovery of the underlying alignment. These are expressed in terms of graph and feature correlation strengths, the number of nodes, and the dimension of the features. Interestingly, whereas an all-or-nothing phase transition is observed in the standard graph-matching scenario, the inclusion of contextual information at the node level introduces a richer structure: the exact-recovery threshold separates from the shared threshold for almost-exact and partial recovery. Closing gaps left by prior works, we provide a sharp characterization of the thresholds governing how structural and contextual information interact in graph matching, and thereby establish a benchmark for designing efficient algorithms in the high-dimensional setting.

items.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention
items.summary: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.

items.title: Improving Mendelian Randomization Analysis by Instrument Borrowing from Auxiliary Outcome Traits
items.summary: Mendelian randomization (MR) infers causal effects of exposures on outcomes using genetic variants as instrumental variables, but existing methods remain vulnerable to bias and loss of power when instruments are invalid. We hypothesize that closely related outcome traits share a large overlap in their valid instruments for a given exposure, so that borrowing instruments across such traits can yield more robust MR inference. To operationalize this, we introduce a novel coheterogeneity statistic, together with its asymptotic theory under different paradigms that allows for a growing number of instruments as the sample size increases, to identify secondary outcome traits likely to share valid instruments with the primary trait. We then propose extensions of two popular methods, MR-Mode and MR-PRESSO, that improve inference for the primary trait by exploiting a secondary trait. Extensive simulations show that the coheterogeneity statistic has the expected finite-sample properties and that instrument-borrowing methods consistently outperform their standard counterparts, with gains increasing as the overlap in valid instruments grows. Applications to established positive and negative control hypotheses indicate improved control of type I error and increased power. We further illustrate practical utility by revisiting the long-debated hypothesis of the causal effect of vitamin D on cardiometabolic traits.

items.title: Learning Topology-Aware Representations for Mechanics-Relevant TPMS Metamaterials
items.summary: Learning informative representations of mechanical Triply Periodic Minimal Surface (TPMS) metamaterials is important for mechanics analysis and structural design, yet existing methods have rarely explicitly supervised learned representations with information about global structural connectivity that is relevant to mechanical response. We propose a topology-aware representation learning framework that integrates persistent homology into a DMAE backbone to explicitly encode global structural connectivity. A persistence-guided masking strategy prioritizes patches associated with persistent topological features, while an auxiliary persistent-homology decoder encourages the latent representation to retain information about topological feature counts across connected components, tunnels, and voids. We evaluate the learned representations on two complementary TPMS datasets using family classification, mechanical-property classification, unsupervised clustering, and regression. Across the two datasets, our method demonstrates strong performance in both structural family and mechanical-property classification, improving family classification by up to 3.9% while achieving the best linear-probe performance. More notably, unsupervised property-clustering performance improves by up to 26.7% and 51.5% across the two datasets, while strong regression performance is retained with $R^2=0.993$. These results establish persistent topology as an effective inductive bias for representation learning of complex three-dimensional mechanical metamaterials.

items.title: Testing Conditional Distribution Equality Using Generative Models
items.summary: Conditional distribution equality testing is a core problem with applications in causal inference, model diagnostics, and transfer learning. Existing methods often lose power when the conditioning variable is high-dimensional. We propose a new test that leverages generative models to compare conditional distributions using both observed data and synthetic samples. A sample-splitting and studentization scheme is introduced to control estimation error. Under the null, the test statistic is asymptotically normal, and we establish local power against contiguous alternatives. Our theory under the null and fixed alternative requires only consistency of the learned conditional distribution, allowing for a broad class of generative models. Empirical results demonstrate accurate size control and strong power in high-dimensional settings compared to representative kernel-based conditional and joint two-sample tests.

items.title: Propensity score with factor loadings: evaluating the effect of the Paris Agreement on the returns of European stocks
items.summary: Factor models for longitudinal data, where policy adoption is unconfounded with respect to a low-dimensional set of latent factor loadings, have become increasingly popular for causal inference. Most existing approaches, however, rely on a causal finite-sample approach or computationally intensive methods, limiting their applicability and external validity. In this paper, we propose a novel method for panel causal inference within a super-population framework, based on inverse propensity score weighting, where the propensity score is a function of latent factor loadings. The approach relaxes the traditional restrictive assumptions of causal panel methods, while offering advantages in terms of causal interpretability, policy relevance, and computational efficiency. Under standard assumptions, we develop a three-step estimation procedure for the ATT and derive its large-sample properties using M-estimation theory. Simulation results show that the proposed estimator remains reliable across a variety of designs, including settings with misspecified factor structure and weakly dependent errors. We apply the method to assess the causal effect of the Paris Agreement - a policy aimed at fostering the transition to a low-carbon economy - on European stock returns. Our empirical results suggest a statistically significant and negative short-run effect on the stock returns of firms that demonstrate a strong commitment to sustainability.

items.title: Bellman Conformal Inference: Calibrating Prediction Intervals For Time Series
items.summary: We introduce Bellman Conformal Inference (BCI), a framework that wraps around any time series forecasting models and provides calibrated prediction intervals. Unlike the existing methods, BCI is able to leverage multi-step ahead forecasts and explicitly optimize the average interval lengths by solving a one-dimensional stochastic control problem (SCP) at each time step. In particular, we use the dynamic programming algorithm to find the optimal policy for the SCP. We prove that BCI achieves long-term coverage under arbitrary distribution shifts and temporal dependence, even with poor multi-step ahead forecasts. When the raw forecast intervals are approximately calibrated, we prove that BCI is near optimal for its surrogate model predictive control problem. We find empirically that BCI avoids uninformative intervals with infinite lengths under our main experimental configuration and generates substantially shorter prediction intervals when the raw forecast intervals are poorly calibrated.

items.title: Tracking a Small Set of Experts in Online Convex Optimization
items.summary: For the fundamental problem of prediction from expert advice, Freund asked whether one could compete with a comparator that switches $k$ times among only $m$ experts. For a discrete set of experts, this problem was resolved by Bousquet and Warmuth (2020), who gave an efficient algorithm with optimal regret matching the information-theoretic limit. We study the analogous problem in online convex optimization, where the action space is continuous. An inefficient algorithm can be derived by discretizing the action space and applying the Bousquet--Warmuth algorithm, giving regret of $\widetilde{O}(md+k)$, while the best known efficient algorithm for this problem has regret $\widetilde{O}(dk)$. We show that this computational inefficiency is inherent, establishing a separation between the information-theoretic and polynomial-time regret achievable for this problem. Specifically, under the hypergraphic planted-clique conjecture, we show that for every polynomial-time algorithm there exist instances for which it incurs at least $(k\sqrt d)^{1-o(1)}$ regret.

items.title: Diminishing Returns of Data in Sparse Autoencoders: Functional Behavior does not Guarantee Feature Reproducibility
items.summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are typically trained on hundreds of millions to billions of activation tokens, yet little work has tested whether this scale is necessary. We study how much activation data SAEs need by training four SAE architectures on three language models with budgets ranging from 5M tokens to a 500M-token reference. We measure two notions of convergence: functional behavior on standard evaluations and one-to-one reproducibility of learned features. Functional data requirements are strongly metric-dependent: reconstruction often approaches the full-data reference at substantially smaller budgets, whereas feature reproducibility continues to improve with data. For Gemma-2-2B BatchTopK, the fraction of strictly matched features rises from 2\% at 5M tokens to 29\% at 50M.
