items.summary: Relying on manipulable characteristics to target the allocation of resources is fraught with difficulties. Naively optimal rules lead to falsification and allocative inefficiency. Optimizing the rule for allocative efficiency while accounting for falsification typically induces falsification, at a heavy cost to the agents. Moreover, falsification generates negative externalities. We characterize optimal falsification-proof rules under a broad range of falsification technologies. We also provide an honesty condition under which they solve the unconstrained problem of a planner who maximizes a weighted sum of allocative surplus and agents' welfare.

items.title: More Goods Means More Commitment
items.summary: A seller without commitment to future offers interacts with a buyer over time. There are many goods for sale, with the buyer's value for a bundle the sum of each bundled good's value. Each date, the seller jointly announces a menu of subsets of the remaining inventory and current prices, and the buyer may purchase one of the offered subsets or wait. In the next period, the seller may again offer any menu of the remaining goods. Neither buyer nor seller can commit to future behavior. I show that as players become maximally patient, if scope increases sufficiently fast compared to patience, revenue per good converges to expected value per good and buyer utility per good converges to zero, in any equilibrium. But if patience instead grows sufficiently fast compared to scope, seller revenue per good converges to the lowest possible value and the buyer captures all remaining surplus, in any equilibrium.

items.title: When One Leak Pays Forever: Context Binding and the Price of Deterring Collusion
items.summary: A coalition that deviates once can profit many times when what it sells keeps working. In a threshold-encrypted mempool, a leading defense against maximal extractable value (MEV), a quorum of the decryption committee that sells its decryption capability to a front-runner exposes every later block that the capability still decrypts. We ask how large a penalty, such as slashable stake, deters this kind of collusion. In our repeated game, a single leak by any coalition in a monotone family of authorized coalitions (for example, any $k$ of the $n$ committee members) unlocks a set of future rounds, costs a one-time penalty, and ends the coalition's participation. We show that every dynamic deviation reduces to choosing a leak time, so deterrence holds if and only if each coalition's penalty covers the largest discounted value that a single leak reaches. Without discounting, over $T$ rounds of unit value full reuse needs a penalty of $T$ while binding each leak to its own round needs $1$, so no penalty that is constant in the horizon deters unbounded reuse; a reuse window of $w$ rounds costs at most $w$ times the largest per-round value. The cheapest profile of per-party stakes that deters every coalition solves a covering linear program. For blockchain design, per-epoch keys cut the required stake from the value of a key's lifetime to the value of one epoch; we calibrate the gap on Ethereum front-running data and place Ferveo and Shutter in the model. The analysis extends to sealed-bid auctions, multi-authority voting, and federated learning under a shared key.

items.title: Screening with Advertisements
items.summary: We investigate a seller's revenue-maximizing mechanism in a setting where a desirable good is sold together with an undesirable bad (e.g., advertisements) that generates third-party revenue. The buyer's private information is two-dimensional: valuation for the good and willingness to pay to avoid the bad. Building on the duality framework of Daskalakis, Deckelbaum, and Tzamos (2017), whose results extend to our setting, we formulate the seller's problem using a transformed measure $μ$ that depends on the third-party payment $k$. We provide a near-characterization for optimality of three pricing mechanisms commonly used in practice -- the Good-Only, Ad-Tiered, and Single-Bundle Posted Price -- and introduce a new class of tractable, interpretable two-dimensional orthant conditions on $μ$ for sufficiency. Economically, $k$ yields a clean comparative static: low $k$ excludes the bad, intermediate $k$ separates ad-tolerant and ad-averse buyers, and high $k$ bundles ads for all types.

items.title: Extracurricular Exercise and Academic Achievement: Evidence from the China Education Panel Survey
items.summary: Does physical exercise enhance adolescent academic achievement, and is there an optimal daily duration? Linking two waves of the China Education Panel Survey ($N=8,247$), we examine this association using restricted cubic splines and classroom fixed effects. Prospective estimates without prior-score controls place non-exercising students 0.162 mean subject-z units below peers exercising one hour daily. Flexible baseline-achievement controls shrink this shortfall by 85.1 percent to 0.024. The exercise block is not jointly significant ($p=0.301$), and curvature tests fail to reject linearity ($p=0.659$). Subgroup estimates yield similar gender profiles, with stronger evidence of location variation in English. These findings establish the importance of academic history in observed exercise gradients and challenge prescriptive exercise targets derived from fitted observational turning points.

items.title: Suspicious Perfection: Rating Rewards, Credibility Inversion, and Information Loss
items.summary: Platforms use rating bonuses and badges to reward good sellers. When ratings can be inflated, stronger rewards can instead weaken the information available to buyers. We study an initially informative rating system in which sellers can pay to raise their displayed score and buyers rationally account for manipulation. Manipulation costs and returns are common across qualities conditional on the honest rating. Under this restriction, credibility can fail to increase between adjacent scores only where the higher score earns an additional reward. Our main result concerns large top-rating bonuses. Once sellers choose only between keeping their honest rating and reaching the top, a larger bonus makes the equilibrium rating system less informative in Blackwell's order along either extremal equilibrium selection. Lower scores retain their honest quality composition but become rarer. As the bonus grows, almost everyone displays the top score, its credibility approaches the population average, and the value of rating information vanishes. Nevertheless, a nearly perfect score can remain more credible than a perfect one. We derive the rate of information loss for exponential manipulation costs and establish a budget-feasible exposure rule that avoids credibility reversals. The results suggest that platform evaluations should examine rating frequencies together with category credibility. Rational buyer skepticism can correct the interpretation of ratings without recovering the distinctions that manipulation has erased.

items.title: Self-ordered choice models
items.summary: Consider an analyst who, for each menu of alternatives, observes a probability distribution over choices, reflecting heterogeneity in the population's choices. The analyst uses a choice model\textendash consisting of deterministic \textit{choice types} \textendash to explain the data, in the sense that mixtures over the admissible types reproduce the observed choice probabilities. A central difficulty is that such representations are typically non-unique. We introduce self-orderedness, a criterion ensuring that every probabilistic choice pattern the analyst can explain admits a unique and ordered representation. We show that self-ordered models are exactly those whose choice types form a \textit{lattice}. This equivalence provides a precise recipe to restrict or extend any choice model for unique ordered representation. Following this recipe, we identify the choice types that are essential for the unique ordered representation of random utility functions. This extension adds economically meaningful non-rational behaviors linked to choice overload and enables identification of the underlying order.

items.title: AI Information Synthesis and Content Polarization
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) can synthesize dispersed information into balanced and informative content, raising the possibility that AI may help reduce polarization. We show that this promise can be undermined by the strategic response of content producers. We develop a game-theoretic model in which consumers acquire information to make downstream decisions, content producers allocate limited informational capacity between broadly valuable vertical information and horizontally differentiated information, and AI provides an alternative source of synthesized information. The effects of AI unfold in three phases as its reliability increases. When reliability is low, AI has no effect on the market. At intermediate levels, AI disciplines prices without attracting consumers or changing content. When AI becomes sufficiently reliable, consumers begin to substitute toward it, and content producers respond by shifting informational capacity away from the vertical dimension and toward horizontally differentiated content, thereby increasing content polarization. The mechanism operates through audience composition: AI attracts consumers who are less well matched to individual producers, leaving producers with stronger incentives to cater to their remaining audiences. The polarization effect intensifies with AI reliability but weakens with greater competition among content producers. Our findings highlight a potential wedge between AI's direct and equilibrium effects: a technology that provides consumers with more balanced information can indirectly make the broader content ecosystem more polarized.

items.title: Maximum score and non-smooth M-estimators with multiway dependence
items.summary: Under i.i.d. sampling, the maximum score estimator of Manski (1975) converges at the cube-root rate to a non-Gaussian limit. We show that, under multiway dependence and low-level conditions, it is asymptotically normal at a parametric rate in the smallest number of clusters and, when the cluster-level variance is non-degenerate, as fast as regular estimators such as probit. The result rests on a general theory for non-smooth M-estimators, under which a modified bootstrap is first-order valid given a consistent Hessian estimate. With two-way clustering, a cube-root term can remain; under high-level conditions, symmetric bootstrap intervals for suitable scalar parameters still control size uniformly.

items.title: Continuity of stable marriage correspondences
items.summary: We study a continuum version of the stable marriage problem, in which each agent has a variable mass to be paired to the opposite side. An agent's mass is interpretable as the divisible time of a single atomistic agent, or as a mass of infinitesimal agents of a particular type. Our object of interest is the mapping between the vector of masses to the set of stable matches. As in the canonical stable marriage model, the set of stable matches can be multi-valued, so this mapping is a correspondence. This correspondence is continuous if and only if the stable match is unique, implying that small changes in the masses may cause discontinuous jumps in the set of stable matches.

items.title: Unit-Demand Pricing for Min-Buying Customers
items.summary: We study the unit-demand pricing problem under \textit{min-buying} behavior, where customers purchase the lowest-priced item that yields non-negative utility. In contrast to the quasi-linear model, we show that uniform pricing becomes substantially more effective under min-buying. First, we study symmetric environments. We show that for min-buying customers with independent and identically distributed valuations, a uniform price across items is optimal. We then extend this optimality result to all valuations drawn from exchangeable and affiliated distributions. However, uniform pricing is not optimal in all symmetric environments: for min-buying customers we construct an exchangeable and non-affiliated valuation distribution for which the gap between uniform pricing and optimal item pricing is logarithmic in the number of items. This gap is tight and matches the worst-case gap in the quasi-linear setting. Next, we consider asymmetric environments in which valuations are independent but not identically distributed. When these valuations are regular and customers are min-buying, we show that a uniform price guarantees approximately 69.86\% of the optimal item-pricing revenue and this is tight. Overall, our results highlight that the value of non-uniform pricing substantially diminishes, and often disappears entirely, under more conservative demand models in which customers engage in satisficing behaviors such as min-buying.

items.title: Creative destruction: Human-AI competition in an experimental market
items.summary: We study two hypotheses for how a human role in production could persist despite growing AI capabilities. Humans might have a durable advantage in taste, designing better products even as AI agents automate routine tasks, or consumers might intrinsically prefer that humans have a hand in production. In our experiment, participants act as producers, designing computer games with an AI coding agent, and as consumers who buy them. Across three studies (N = 1,025), we find no evidence for either hypothesis. Games designed by an AI on its own outperform those of human producers, including both amateurs and professional creatives. Human producers do not anticipate the AI's advantage. Revealing whether a game is human-designed does not raise consumers' willingness to pay for the product.

items.title: Pricing Intelligence: Task-Based Learning and Labor Displacement in the AI Economy
items.summary: What determines the speed of AI-driven labor displacement? I study this question in a microeconomic model in which users choose between labor and AI to complete tasks of different complexity. Profit-maximizing AI providers set the price of AI, and AI systems improve through task-specific learning from deployment. In an initial technological state where labor has the comparative advantage at complex tasks, the providers' profit maximization incentives suppress AI deployment on complex tasks, even though these are most valuable for frontier learning. I characterize when this tension gives rise to an accelerating path of AI adoption or a learning trap. Competition can accelerate AI adoption relative to monopoly by shifting AI deployment toward more complex tasks, which boosts frontier learning. Asymmetric competition can further accelerate AI adoption by inducing providers to specialize, which concentrates complex-task data.

items.title: Large player classes and approximately weighted voting
items.summary: It is known that completeness of the coalitional ($C$-)desirability relation in a simple game does not imply the existence of a weighted-majority representation. We show that weightedness is implied in an approximate sense. Call an $n$-player simple game $\varepsilon$-weighted if, for some weight vector in the $(n-1)$-simplex, any losing coalition weight exceeds any winning coalition weight by at most $\varepsilon$; let $\varepsilon^{\ast}$ be the smallest such $\varepsilon$. We establish an upper bound on $\varepsilon^{\ast}$ in a general $C$-complete game, and deduce that, if all classes of equally desirable players become large asymptotically but the number of classes is bounded, then $\varepsilon^{\ast}=O(1/n_{\min})$ for the minimal player class size $n_{\min}$, and the bound is tight. Importantly, the minimal attainable fraction $δ$ of coalitions mislabeled by a weighting rule also tends to $0$ when $n_{\min}\rightarrow\infty$ and the number of player classes is bounded, with $δ=O(1/\sqrt{n_{\min}})$.

items.title: Bootstrap Adaptive Lasso Solution Path Unit Root Tests
items.summary: We propose sieve wild bootstrap analogues to the adaptive Lasso solution path unit root tests of Arnold and Reinschlüssel (2024) arXiv:2404.06205 to improve finite sample properties and extend their applicability to a generalised framework, allowing for non-stationary volatility. Numerical evidence shows the bootstrap to improve the tests' precision for error processes that promote spurious rejections of the unit root null, depending on the detrending procedure. The bootstrap mitigates finite-sample size distortions and restores asymptotically valid inference when the data features time-varying unconditional variance. We apply the bootstrap tests to real residential property prices of the top six Eurozone economies and find evidence of stationarity to be period-specific, supporting the conjecture that exuberance in the housing market characterises the development of Euro-era residential property prices in the recent past.

items.title: Dynamic Panel Multinomial Logit Models
items.summary: This paper provides moment conditions for dynamic multinomial logit panel data models with individual specific fixed effects. The moment conditions do not depend on the fixed effects and thus form the basis for generalized method of moments estimation. For a leading case, we provide sufficient conditions under which the moment conditions identify the common parameters, and we illustrate their use in an empirical application to household soft drink purchases. The construction of moment conditions is based on transformed models obtained by permuting outcomes across time periods. For any cyclic permutation, the ratio of the transformed model probability to the true model probability is free of the fixed effects, and comparing two such ratios yields restrictions on the common parameters of interest. This construction is not specific to the multinomial logit. It applies to any dynamic panel data model whose static counterpart admits a symmetric sufficient statistic for the fixed effects. This unifies our main result with analogous results for other models.

items.title: The Limits of Tolerance
items.summary: I propose a model of aggregation of intervals relevant to the study of legal standards of tolerance. Using this model, I introduce the family of endpoint rules, which aggregate intervals according to the p-th lowest lower endpoint and the q-th highest upper endpoint. This family includes extreme tolerance (allowing anything permitted by anyone) and a form of majoritarianism (the median rule). I show that the family of endpoint rules is characterized by both the combination of anonymity, responsiveness, continuity, and ordinal neutrality, and the combination of anonymity, strategyproofness, and translation equivariance.

items.title: Information-Enriched Selection of Stationary and Non-Stationary Autoregressions using the Adaptive Lasso
items.summary: We propose a novel approach to elicit the weight of a potentially non-stationary regressor in the consistent and oracle-efficient estimation of autoregressive models using the adaptive Lasso. The enhanced weight builds on a statistic that exploits distinct orders in probability of the OLS estimator in time series regressions when the degree of integration differs. We provide theoretical results on the benefit of our approach for detecting stationarity when a tuning criterion selects the $\ell_1$ penalty parameter. Monte Carlo evidence shows that our proposal is superior to using OLS-based weights, as suggested by Kock [Econom. Theory, 32, 2016, 243-259]. We apply the modified estimator to model selection for German inflation rates after the introduction of the Euro. The results indicate that energy commodity price inflation and headline inflation are best described by stationary autoregressions.

items.title: Media Slant is Contagious
items.summary: This paper examines the diffusion of media slant. We document the influence of Fox News Channel (FNC) on the partisan slant of local newspapers in the U.S. over the years 1995-2008. We measure the political slant of local newspapers by scaling the news article texts to Republicans' and Democrats' speeches in Congress. Using channel positioning as an instrument for viewership, we find that higher FNC viewership causes local newspapers to adopt more right-wing slant. The effect emerges gradually, only several years after FNC's introduction, mirroring the channel's growing influence on voting behaviour. A main driver of the shift in newspaper slant appears to be a change in local political preferences.

items.title: Better together? A performance theory of human-machine skill policies under generalization difficulty
items.summary: Organizations pairing a human and a machine on a task decide, often by default, which executes each instance and what happens when both do. We account for what this attains under the squared rule, with performance distributed over instances to capture generalization difficulty. A gross stake lies between the skills' mean and best per instance. It splits at the best single skill into a systematic part, known from separate assessments and secured by commitment, and a residual, the expected value of perfect information on which skill each instance favors, known only from paired observation and split further by classes. Skills set the stake; workflows decide the take, via two channels. Routing directs work, weighting or selecting responses; with binary truth it is capped by the best skill per instance. Reading responses as joint evidence is not routing; what they jointly reveal caps it. Synergy lets skills interact before responding; bounded by no skill either way, its lift over independent responses must clear a break-even and can fall below one. As algorithms, arrangements form a ladder stating what each reads, holds and records, and a procedure whose checks keep earlier gains when class means are known and lose little on finite records given a margin. The theory extends to many skills, each worth what it adds where it beats all others held, and to competing skills, where at parity a single failure's allowed cost decides. In a public chest-radiograph study with 227 radiologists, they are near parity with the model and the stake is mostly residual; assisted reading, no better on average originally, returned less than averaging both responses; recalibrating the model alone beats any deployable arrangement of raw responses. Organizations can learn from their records what is at stake, which arrangement collects it and what evidence each step needs; pricing costs and errors is future work.

items.title: Agentic Workflows for Economic Research: Design, Implementation, and Evaluation
items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) can now assist across the economic research lifecycle, yet general-purpose LLMs and agent systems give no assurance that their outputs meet the discipline's bar. We present an agentic-workflow methodology that carries a research question through the full lifecycle, from ideation and literature review through modeling, data, implementation, estimation, and reporting, across seven specialized teams under a cross-team orchestrator, with human-in-the-loop review at each stage. The methodology incorporates two commitments. The first, trustworthy execution, is a shared infrastructure that verifies outputs, records the provenance of every step, bounds each agent's authority, addresses agent-specific threats, and serves every LLM locally on open weights. The second, reasoning as an economist, makes disciplinary checks explicit in the workflow: agents state identification strategies for causal claims, check structural models against stylized facts by simulation, and search for counterexamples to theoretical claims. Together they produce a first research prototype in hours, with every step's provenance and verification verdict recorded. A two-tier framework evaluates the workflows across fourteen dimensions, combining execution-log metrics with a dual-judge LLM-as-reviewer ensemble across all seven teams.

items.title: Does the Gender Wage Gap Originate at Labor Market Entry? Evidence from South Korea
items.summary: When in the lifecycle does a large gender wage gap emerge? South Korea has the largest aggregate gender pay gap (29%) in the OECD. Among recent college graduates the conditional gap is only 3.3% over 2008-2019, falling from 3.4% to 2.5%. Correcting for differential selection into employment with semiparametric and machine learning methods leaves it unchanged. Nonparametric and semiparametric bounds contain the point estimates. Selection-corrected quantile regression shows that the remaining entry-level gap is concentrated at the top of the distribution. In Korean panel data the corrected gap widens severalfold across the prime-age workforce, where the selection correction becomes first order. Korea's gender wage disparity is mostly generated after labor market entry.

items.title: Difference-in-Differences Estimators When No Unit Remains Untreated
items.summary: We study difference-in-differences designs in which all units are initially untreated and later receive heterogeneous, strictly positive treatment doses. When quasi-untreated units receive doses close to zero, a difference-in-difference estimand using those units as the control group identifies a weighted average treatment effect per unit of treatment, under a parallel-trends assumption. We develop a nonparametric estimator and bias-corrected confidence intervals for this parameter. We also show that the assumptions justifying the usual two-way fixed-effects estimator imply testable linearity restrictions, and propose specification tests that can guide its use.

items.title: Pseudo-Panel Event Studies: Econometric Foundations for Credible Applications
items.summary: Event studies with panel data are widely used to estimate treatment effects. With repeated cross-sections, future treatment dates are unobserved for untreated individuals. Pseudo-panel event studies impute pre-treatment outcomes of the treated using matched untreated individuals. This paper establishes identification in such designs and characterizes bias when identification conditions fail. I show that the pseudo-panel regression is equivalent to weighted least squares with group means. This representation simplifies computation and yields analytical inference. In simulations, analytical confidence intervals attain near-nominal coverage, whereas conventional intervals substantially undercover. I also develop a doubly robust estimator using richer covariates, a symmetric matching design with synthetic type fixed effects, and a fully nonparametric estimator that accommodates heterogeneous treatment effects. In a Korean panel survey, the pseudo-panel regression yields an employment child penalty of 42.1%, close to 46.9% in the actual panel. Applications to repeated cross-sections yield employment penalties of about one-third.

items.title: Testing for an Explosive Bubble using High-Frequency Volatility
items.summary: Based on a continuous-time stochastic volatility model with a linear drift, we develop a test for explosive behavior in financial asset prices at a low frequency when prices are sampled at a higher frequency. The test exploits the volatility information in the high-frequency data. The method consists of devolatizing log-asset price increments with realized volatility measures and performing a supremum-type recursive Dickey-Fuller test on the devolatized sample. The proposed test has a nuisance-parameter-free asymptotic distribution and is easy to implement. We study the size and power properties of the test in Monte Carlo simulations. A real-time date-stamping strategy based on the devolatized sample is proposed for the origination and conclusion dates of the explosive regime. Conditions under which the real-time date-stamping strategy is consistent are established. The test and the date-stamping strategy are applied to study explosive behavior in cryptocurrency and stock markets.

items.title: Estimation of Rational Inattention--Additive Random Utility Models
items.summary: This paper develops likelihood-based estimation for parametric rational inattention--additive random utility models. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the exact maximum likelihood estimator and provide conditions under which the simulated estimator shares its asymptotic distribution. To implement estimation, we develop Newton--BA, a KKT-guided hybrid of Newton--Raphson and Blahut--Arimoto (BA). The algorithm accommodates both interior and boundary solutions and substantially improves computational efficiency relative to direct BA while preserving numerical accuracy. Monte Carlo simulations show that parameter recovery improves with sample size and that confidence-interval coverage is generally close to the nominal $95$ percent level. Finally, we compare our model with no- and perfect-information logit benchmarks in an empirically calibrated ModeCanada experiment. Our model achieves similar in-sample likelihood fit to perfect-information logit but more accurately recovers key preference parameters, choice probabilities, and responses to travel-time changes.

items.title: Honest Inference for High-Dimensional Linear Models
items.summary: We propose a heteroskedasticity-robust and dimention-adaptive test for multiple linear restric- tions in sparse high-dimensional linear regression models. It combines desparsified LASSO estimation with a ridge-regularized quadratic form statistic and critical values that adapt to the restriction dimension. Under stated regularity conditions, our approach is asymptotically valid under a fixed or diverging number of restrictions without specifying the asymptotic regime in advance. Our random-design theory allows independent non-identically distributed covari- ate rows with marginal sub-Weibull tails and heteroskedastic errors satisfying finite polynomial moments. Monte Carlo simulations demonstrate improved finite-sample size control relative to conventional Wald tests, particularly as the number of restrictions increases.

items.title: The Myth of Restrictive Working-Time Agreements: Firms' Working-Time Adjustment after Exit from Collective Bargaining
items.summary: Employers in Germany argue that collective agreements restrict their flexibility concerning working hours. Using data from the IAB Establishment Panel for the years 2008 to 2024, we investigate working-time adjustments after exit from collective bargaining. We find that exit is associated with only a modest increase in weekly working hours of around 0.3 to 0.6 per cent using fixed-effects and event-study models, corresponding to eight to thirteen additional minutes per week. This adjustment occurs shortly after leaving collective bargaining coverage. We further find no evidence that other margins of working-time adjustment, such as Saturday or Sunday work, are used more extensively after exit. In contrast to previous survey evidence, our findings call into question that working-hours constraints are one of the main drivers of exit from collective bargaining coverage.

items.title: Identity-Compatible Auctions
items.summary: This paper studies sellers' and buyers' incentives to engage in shill bidding in single-object auctions. An auction is seller identity-compatible if the seller cannot profit by posing as one or more bidders through fictitious identities, and buyer identity-compatible if no buyer can profit by posing as multiple bidders. We distinguish lit auctions, which reveal the number of bidders, from dark auctions, which conceal it. Our results highlight the importance of concealing the number of bidders in deterring shill bidding: no optimal lit auction can achieve our design goal, whereas the dark first-price auction uniquely does.

items.title: Are Higher Suspicious Transaction Report Volumes Associated with More Future Money-Laundering Convictions?
items.summary: Almost all countries require banks to file suspicious transaction reports (STRs) to help authorities detect and prosecute money laundering. The number of STRs filed in a country is an often-cited metric in international anti-money laundering (AML) compliance evaluations. However, it remains unclear if the volume of STRs filed in a country is associated with the country's future number of money laundering convictions. Using data from Europol, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund, and the European Sourcebook of Crime and Criminal Justice Statistics, we examine if STR volumes can be associated with future money-laundering conviction volumes in countries in the European Union. Our analysis employs pooled and fixed-effects regression models with one- to five-year lags, controlling for population sizes, shadow-economy estimates, and police force sizes. In our pooled and country-specific fixed-effects models, STR volumes appear to be positively associated with future convictions. However, the association weakens and becomes insignificant when we control for both country-specific and common time effects. Our results provide a caution against assuming that STR volumes, by themselves, are reliable indicators of future money-laundering convictions and, to the extent convictions reflect outcomes, AML effectiveness.

items.title: Measuring Concept Content in Text from LLM Activations: ESG Evidence from Concept Vectors and Linear Probes
items.summary: Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) encode more information in their activations than they show in their responses. We ask whether the information contained in activations could be used as a source of measurement for the presence of concepts. We compare two algorithms for extraction of concepts, i.e., Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm and linear probing against an embedding baseline, surface baselines, and the model's own response using a human-annotated Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) dataset of financial texts. The best linear probe ranges from 0.6 to 3.3 percentage points below fine-tuned domain classifiers. The probes also outscore the model's own response in all comparisons. Furthermore, the probes outperform the RFM concept vectors in all accuracy comparisons. In a synthetic mixture test, their mean-pooled score tracks the number of concept sentences in a paragraph better than the concept-vector score. Put together, a linear probe on a frozen LLM is a cost-effective and generalizable alternative to fine-tuning a domain classifier.

items.title: Local Strategy-proofness and Dictatorship
items.summary: We investigate preference domains on which every unanimous and locally strategy-proof social choice function (scf) is dictatorial. We identify a condition on domains, connected with distinct neighbours, that is necessary for this property. We then show that the condition is also sufficient on L-tops-only domains, i.e., domains on which every unanimous and locally strategy-proof scf is tops-only. Whether every connected with distinct neighbours domain is L-tops-only remains open; if some are not, our sufficiency result is silent on them. We show, however, that every connected with distinct neighbours domain, L-tops-only or not, is a dictatorial domain, i.e., unanimity and strategy-proofness (a stronger requirement than local strategy-proofness) force dictatorship on it.

items.title: Inference on the Value of Policy Improvement in Adaptive Experiments
items.summary: In this paper, we develop an asymptotically normal estimator for the value of policy improvement (VPI) under adaptively collected data. This value, which is defined as the gap between the value of the best treatment policy in a class and that of a baseline policy, gauges whether or not it is worth deploying a personalized treatment policy. Building an estimator for the VPI is naturally more difficult than estimating the value of a fixed policy. This is because, in addition to contending with the correlated data and decaying propensities associated with adaptive experiments, any estimator must also handle the non-regularity, or lack of pathwise differentiability, of the underlying estimand when the optimal policy is non-unique. Our proposed estimator works by sequentially fitting a weighted empirical welfare maximizing policy on historical data and then evaluating it using inverse propensity weighting on future samples. We neither assume that the optimal policy is unique nor make a margin assumption on the underlying heterogeneous treatment effects. A key difficulty in analyzing our estimator is showing that the regret incurred through policy learning is asymptotically smaller than the standard error of the estimator. We accomplish this by showing faster regret rates for policy learning under decaying propensities, which may be of independent interest. We not only evaluate the coverage of our estimator on a mix of synthetic and semi-synthetic data, but also employ it to estimate the VPI in an adaptive experiment evaluating the efficacy of job assistance programs in Jordan due to Caria et al. Although our estimates are generally more conservative than their hierarchical Bayesian analysis, which assumes that the optimal policy is unique, we still corroborate the benefits of personalization amongst Syrian refugees.

items.title: Resource Allocation with Midterm Review
items.summary: A principal funds an agent's project over two periods, with a midterm review providing a public signal about project quality. The agent privately knows the project's quality and always prefers more funding, while the principal wants to match funding to quality. A natural benchmark uses the review only after it arrives, to update beliefs and improve the second-period allocation. The optimal mechanism instead frontloads the review's information value: it also uses the review as an incentive device to elicit truthful reporting up front, thereby strictly improving the principal's first-period expected payoff. In the optimal mechanism, higher-quality projects receive more funding initially but face larger cuts after a bad review, leaving them with less funding than lower-quality projects. A good review increases funding, but the resulting allocation need not preserve the initial ranking of projects and eventually declines with quality.

items.title: A Robust Electric Vehicle Charging Station Optimization under Rare Event Disruptions
items.summary: The rising demand for electric vehicles (EVs) requires robust and accessible charging infrastructure, particularly in developing countries where frequent electricity disruptions pose a significant service-reliability risk. Prior charging-infrastructure optimization studies rarely address such disruptions rigorously, yielding suboptimal and fragile designs. We present a simulation-based optimization model that estimates each candidate station's service reliability and embeds it directly in the objective and constraints, framing charging-network design as an engineering-management decision under uncertainty. To make the approach computationally tractable, we apply the control variates (CV) variance-reduction technique to the reliability estimation. Using a real dataset from Surabaya, Indonesia, our numerical experiment shows that the proposed robust model achieves a 13% higher average objective value than the non-robust benchmark and remains robust even when station reliability is under- or over-estimated. The CV technique reduces the required simulation sample size by up to a factor of 10 relative to Monte Carlo, allowing the model to be solved efficiently with a standard mixed-integer programming (MIP) solver.

items.title: Uncertainty in Compound Decisions
items.summary: Researchers and policymakers frequently make a large number of decisions simultaneously over many units using noisy estimates of unit-level effects. Researchers often assume that unit-level effects are drawn from a common effect distribution, allowing for optimal decision-making. In applications, however, this effect distribution is unknown to the econometrician, introducing uncertainty in the ultimate decision-making problem. This paper considers the problem of quantifying this uncertainty. For instance, researchers may seek to understand how an oracle decision maker with knowledge of the effect distribution would compare different feasible decisions, or understand which decisions an oracle would plausibly make. Analyzing these questions from the perspective of an oracle decision maker involves comparing the conditional means of unit-level effects given estimates thereof, suggesting a sufficient inferential objective of uniform coverage of these conditional means. Based on an equivalence between uniform coverage of conditional means and multiple testing, I develop methods that satisfy this coverage. Finally, I consider an application to the problem of identifying high-economic-mobility neighborhoods. My methods sharpen inference relative to existing methods and identify units that can be confidently included in oracle selections.

items.title: Valid Inference After Control Selection in Difference-in-Differences
items.summary: We develop the first empirically implementable selective-inference framework for difference-in-differences with controls selected by pre-treatment fit. We construct confidence intervals for the average treatment effect on the treated (ATT), incorporating that selection and estimating the unknown full covariance from the same observations. Counterexamples establish undercoverage from Roth's fixed-comparison pretest adjustment and direct Gaussian-score application of Andrews--Kitagawa--McCloskey to this selection, despite parallel trends for every candidate. Retaining the actual polynomial or piecewise-polynomial event, we establish uniform validity at perfect fit and population ties, endpoint equivalence with known-covariance inference, and unequal-sample guarantees. We accommodate staggered adoption, reused observations, and fitting-rule choice. In police-deployment and minimum-wage reanalyses, we find changes in significance and economically relevant effect ranges while retaining the selected comparison. For a smooth randomized test, we obtain higher-order accuracy through stabilized joint mean--covariance correction preserving normal-sampling baseline rejection probabilities. Researchers should disclose selection rules alongside ATT uncertainty.

items.title: Persuasion under the Threat of Verification
items.summary: This paper studies persuasion when public information is costly and receivers can verify the state before acting. Verification may overturn acceptance after favorable public news, but it may also induce acceptance after unfavorable news. We characterize how these two effects shape the sender's optimal experiment. Cheaper verification can lead the sender to disclose less and rely more on receivers' own discoveries, thereby increasing its payoff. With heterogeneous decision thresholds, we identify exact conditions for the disclosure response and show why it depends on the distribution of preferences. In a separate parameter region, cheaper verification increases inspection but reduces every threshold type's final information and welfare; the sender also loses. We then allow receivers to share their findings. Cheaper inspection and wider sharing can move optimal public disclosure in opposite directions, even when both benefit the sender. Wider sharing can also reduce aggregate final information while improving every threshold type's welfare. The results distinguish the effects of verification on public disclosure, information ultimately obtained, and the cost of obtaining it.

items.title: Eigenvalue-Decomposition Cost Denoising for Predict-then-Optimize
items.summary: Predict-then-optimize methods learn a mapping from features to unknown edge costs. They then solve the shortest-path problem on the predicted costs. We study a feature-free alternative for the case where the decision-maker observes many noisy cost vectors on a fixed network. The cost vectors are denoised by an eigenvalue decomposition (PCA) of their covariance matrix. Dijkstra's algorithm then runs on the result. We test this on the $5\times5$ grid of \citet{elmachtoub2022}, with $1000$ independent replications and a fresh ground truth in each. We compare against SPO+, against naive Dijkstra on noisy costs, and against two alternatives to a hand-picked rank $k$ (the Gavish-Donoho threshold and a Ledoit-Wolf filter). We also test a hybrid of SPO+ and PCA. Four findings emerge. First, the rank matters. Keeping $k=2$ components performs worse than no denoising. Second, when costs are close to linear in the features, the Gavish-Donoho threshold recovers the true rank without supervision. PCA-denoised Dijkstra outperforms SPO+ at $°=1$, but underperforms SPO+ at $°\geq 2$. The hybrid works best at $°=1$ and is slightly better than SPO+ at $°=2$. Third, when costs are strongly nonlinear ($°=4$), the signal is no longer low-rank, and only the Ledoit-Wolf filter clearly beats the naive baseline. Fourth, the benefit of denoising grows with network size on grids, but not on a layered non-grid network at high nonlinearity.

items.title: Web3 x AI Agents: Landscape, Integrations, and Foundational Challenges
items.summary: The convergence of Web3 technologies and AI agents is a rapidly evolving frontier that is reshaping decentralized ecosystems. This paper presents the first comprehensive landscape analysis of the intersection between Web3 and AI agents, examining five critical dimensions: landscape, economics, governance, security, and trust mechanisms. Through an analysis of 979 capitalized Web3-AI agent tokens at a 1 September 2026 cutoff, compared with a cohort of 275 tokens collected at 6 April 2025, we develop a taxonomy and systematically map the current market landscape (RQ1), identifying distinct patterns in project distribution and capitalization. We complement the token frame with on-chain measurement of the agent standards layer: 530,266 ERC-8004 identity registrations across 16 chains and 432,913 x402 settlements on Base. We then investigate four integration domains: AI agents in decentralized finance (RQ2), governance (RQ3), security (RQ4), and Web3 trust mechanisms for agent reliability (RQ5). Infrastructure dominates the landscape in both project count and capitalization; value is highly concentrated (Gini 0.938), and the archived cohort lost 36.4% in capitalization over seventeen months despite token population growth. The agent standards layer shows adoption at scale, but economic throughput remains limited. Across integration domains, AI agents extend DeFi trading and make continuous security auditing affordable, while agents in governance remain largely a blueprint. These findings outline critical considerations for future research toward robust, intelligent, and trustworthy decentralized systems with AI agent interactions.

items.title: Recurrent Neural Networks for Forecasting Autoregressive Noncausal Processes
items.summary: This paper examines the use of recurrent neural networks and their extensions for forecasting autoregressive causal-noncausal processes, characterized by local explosive patterns such as bubbles and spikes. We study the recurrent neural networks (RNN), long short-term memory networks (LSTM), gated recurrent unit (GRU), bidirectional LSTM, and also a simple feed-forward network (FNN) to reveal the difficulty of forecasting extreme values depending on the type of network and the length of the training set. We show that FNN outperforms other networks in predicting extreme values of a univariate noncausal time series during a bubble. We also examine the improvements of point predictions of extreme values resulting from pooling and a modified loss function.

items.title: Dynamic Mechanism and Information Design in AI-Agent Environments: A General Analytical Framework
items.summary: This paper develops a general framework for dynamic mechanism and information design with AI agents, encompassing optimal contracting and integrating evolving hidden information and hidden action with partial verification, technological authorization, and multi-agent interaction. It nests conventional dynamic screening, hidden-action contracting, and conditional dynamic information design, while allowing reporting, action, and information-use decisions to interact through a common continuation mechanism. We establish a dynamic revelation principle and a recursive characterization of implementability in which truthful reporting and post-report obedience are jointly determined through continuation incentives. In quasilinear optimal-contracting environments, dynamic envelope and integral-monotonicity methods yield a verification-adjusted dynamic virtual-surplus representation and identify three distinct margins: dynamic information rents, verification rents, and the implementation cost of hidden action. These margins generate a branched hierarchy separating conventional dynamic screening, hidden-action contracting, and their joint problem. We also study the joint design of monitoring, information use, and incentives: more informative monitoring capacity expands the designer's opportunity set, but full disclosure need not be optimal, and information use can itself alter hidden-action incentives. With multiple agents, correlated information, peer discipline, coupled incentives, joint feasibility, and continuation opportunities create additional strategic interactions. Although motivated by AI-agent environments, the framework applies more broadly to dynamic agency settings with similar economic features.

items.title: GMM under finite-population asymptotics: instrumental variables and regression adjustment
items.summary: This paper extends the finite-population asymptotic framework of Abadie et al. (2014,2020) to the generalized method of moments (GMM) estimator for moment condition models. Motivating examples include instrumental variable regressions and regression adjustments under randomized controlled trials. We establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the GMM estimator and propose conservative variance estimators. We also study GMM weighting, misspecification, and over-identification testing under finite-population asymptotics. Notably, even though the optimally weighted GMM estimator is infeasible under finite-population asymptotics, the regression adjustment estimator in a randomized controlled trial is shown to be asymptotically equivalent to the optimally weighted GMM estimator. A simulation study and real data application illustrate the usefulness of our GMM theory.

items.title: Endogenous Vindication: Reputation and Effort in Expert Advice
items.summary: Does making advice cheaper to implement increase the supply of advice? We study an expert who can release a favorable certificate to a sequence of clients. Implementation requires the certificate, and its outcome depends on client effort. The expert values client surplus and career income from routine employment; ability is unknown to both the expert and the public. A lower fixed implementation cost weakly increases both advice and client surplus. A lower marginal effort cost can have the opposite effect: greater effort makes failure more revealing and can induce the expert to withhold advice permanently. We establish this reversal for every discount factor on an open family with smooth income utility with constant absolute risk aversion. At a common initial reputation, cheaper effort then eliminates public learning and client surplus. The reversal is impossible when the effort rule is held fixed across the same cost change. Rare outside reports preserve the discounted client-surplus reversal, although recurrent informative reports restore eventual learning. Additional shape restrictions yield a reputation cutoff; without them, advice can be disconnected and even success can stop further evaluation.

items.title: AI Model Design and Physician Liability
items.summary: Clinical algorithms can perform differently across patient groups, a concern that grows as these algorithms increasingly take the form of artificial intelligence (AI) models. In the United States, a 2024 federal rule bars healthcare providers that receive federal funds from discriminating through their use of clinical algorithms, which exposes them to liability when such use disadvantages a protected patient group. We examine how such liability considerations reshape (i) an AI firm's model design decisions that drive group-specific accuracy and (ii) a physician's decisions to use AI in healthcare delivery. The firm designs an AI model for two patient groups, and improving accuracy for the disadvantaged group is more costly. The physician (who remains the accountable decision maker) then decides whether to consult AI, weighing the reduction in clinical uncertainty against expected liability exposure when AI errors disproportionately affect the disadvantaged group. We find that this liability can induce disparate use of AI: the physician may reduce AI use overall and, over an intermediate range of liability, rely on AI less for disadvantaged patients. The effect is non-monotone. As liability increases, the physician's use of AI for disadvantaged patients first declines, then rises as the firm reallocates investment toward reducing disparity or switches to an equal-accuracy design. Mandating equal algorithmic accuracy across patient groups can then inadvertently harm both groups, because a uniform accuracy requirement distorts the firm's investment incentives and the physician's equilibrium AI-use decisions.

items.title: Randomized Experiments with Ambiguous Record Linkage
items.summary: Randomized experiments are often linked to administrative data to measure outcomes, but coarse identifiers can leave multiple administrative records consistent with each experimental unit. We show that unbiased estimation of the sample average treatment effect is possible without resolving these ambiguous links or specifying an outcome model. Our key linkage requirement is that the true administrative outcome is contained among the candidate outcomes for each experimental unit. We characterize the precision cost of linkage ambiguity and study two complementary ways to mitigate it: regression adjustment and reweighting based on observed linkage characteristics. We establish finite-sample and asymptotic properties of these estimators and develop valid randomization-based and large-sample inference.

items.title: Too Late to Prune: Generative AI, the Screen, and Team Creative Decisions
items.summary: Generative AI makes options cheap and shifts the bottleneck of creative work from generating options to screening them. We argue that AI's value depends on whether its options arrive before or after the team's screen. In our model, early options compete for a place in the portfolio; late options arrive after that competition and are kept unscreened. In a preregistered experiment, we randomly assigned 148 three-person teams to five schedules of access to the same language model during a product-design task with timed search and selection stages. Moving the same 15 minutes of access from search to selection lowered expert-rated creativity by 0.62 standard deviations, although teams used the model at similar rates. Platform logs locate the difference at the screen. Early access enlarged the pool of ideas fivefold, and teams pruned it. Late-access teams reached the screen with the same small pool as teams without AI and then searched again, devoting 29% of their selection-stage queries to generating new options, compared with 11% for teams with access throughout. Late access added breadth, not quality: these teams submitted 73% more proposals than did teams without AI. Language-model judges detected the benefit of access but not the cost of late timing.

items.title: Optimal Transport in Economics
items.summary: Optimal transport provides a common language for allocation, equilibrium, computation, and inference. Its primal problem assigns mass or agents, while its dual variables admit economic interpretations as utilities, prices, and scarcity rents. This review explains why this combination has proved unusually effective in economics. We first present the core results, including Kantorovich duality, integrality, cyclical monotonicity, the canonical distance and quadratic costs, and entropic regularization. We then trace the field's development from planning and operations research to modern analysis, statistics, and computation. The economic literature is organized around two roles for transport: as a model of matching, trade, hedonic equilibrium, and aggregate assignment; and as a tool for coupling distributions, measuring discrepancies, constructing multivariate ranks, solving inverse problems, and certifying economic conclusions. We conclude by examining extensions beyond transferable utility, one-to-one matching, static allocation, and unconstrained transport, together with open questions involving learning and identification across multiple markets.

items.title: Global Automation Atlas
items.summary: Automation can displace or complement labour, but this need not be constant across economies. Existing exposure measures typically assign fixed scores to tasks or occupations and capture cross-country variation through employment structure. We posit that exposure to automation depends jointly on task content and country-level conditions. We use a large language model to classify 18,797 work tasks in 124 economies by exposure, labour margin, technology channel and artificial-intelligence materiality. Country conditioning changes the classification of the same task and the occupation exposure rankings, especially in lower-income economies. Country-conditioned scores improve out-of-country predictions of firms' production-technology use and AI adoption; physical-execution exposure tracks industrial-robot use and density, while Atlas scores align with observed work-related ChatGPT and Claude use across activities and countries. The share of tasks exposed to automation ranges from 3.3% to 61.6% across countries. It rises with income but varies considerably within income groups. Lower-income economies are more concentrated in rule-based and labour-substituting forms of automation, whereas physical execution, planning and inference channels, together with labour-augmenting uses of artificial intelligence, become more prominent with development. Combined with employment data, we find that women are disproportionately employed in occupations with substitution-facing exposure. Across countries, higher informality is associated with a smaller exposed-task share but a larger substitution-only share among exposed tasks. Machine-learning hypothesis generation methods point to both economic and institutional drivers: automation is more feasible where firms have machinery, digital records and connected systems, but less so where tasks depend on local knowledge and trusted relationships.

items.title: Displacement Is Endogenous: AI Workers in a Search-and-Matching Labor Market
items.summary: We build a labor market in which AI systems enter as workers: they apply for jobs, pass screenings, get hired, and get dismissed, alongside humans. Firms post vacancies, workers search with friction, and product demand slopes downward. Across 30 seeded runs per configuration, AI entry at 70% of the human wage raises unemployment by 4.1 percentage points (95% CI 3.5 to 4.6) and leaves 12.2 fewer humans employed (CI 10.5 to 13.9). Layoffs dominate when AI is much cheaper than humans: the layoff margin accounts for 7.2 of the lost jobs and reduced hiring for 5.0, though most dismissed workers find work again. A wider price gap reduces displacement, because cheap AI makes firms expand: at price parity, with zero dismissals, the unemployment effect is largest at 9.2 points (CI 8.6 to 9.9), all of it through hiring. That parity result survives cutting AI applications from five per period to one. Demand elasticity decides how many workers AI displaces. Screening changes who gets hired and leaves the displacement total unchanged.

items.title: From Observation to Intervention: Mastering Bus Holding Control from Historical Uncontrolled Trajectories with Offline Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Bus operations are inherently unstable---buses initially dispatched at equal headways will inevitably end up bunching up. This issue exacerbates passenger waiting times, creates load imbalances between buses, and undermines service reliability. Reinforcement learning (RL) has proven highly effective for mitigating bus bunching and outperforms traditional model-based approaches. However, existing RL approaches require agents to continuously interact with the environment, which potentially disrupts the bus system before effective policies are learned. This paper proposes an Offline Graph-based Multi-agent Actor-Critic (Offline-GMAC) method that trains bus holding policies using only readily available logged GPS data collected during normal uncontrolled operations, thereby eliminating the need for disruptive online interaction or exploration. The method employs general graph neural networks for multi-agent credit assignment. A key innovation of our method is a data augmentation scheme that synthesizes unperformed holding actions from historical uncontrolled bus trajectories. The scheme exploits the equivalence between stochastic link travel time delays and deliberate holding interventions. Under mild assumptions, we prove that the 1-Wasserstein distance between synthesized and target state transition distributions is bounded above by a term that scales linearly with the standard deviation of link travel times plus a tunable synthesis-dependent term. Evaluations using real-world bus data demonstrate that the proposed offline method achieves performance comparable to, and in some cases, even better than its online counterpart.

items.title: Cointegrated Regressors: Where Folded Concave Penalties Go Beyond LASSO
items.summary: LASSO is one of the most popular regularization methods for high-dimensional regression models. While cointegration is common in practical applications of predictive regressions with many regressors, the convex penalty of LASSO overly suppresses the coefficients of cointegrated regressors and therefore fails to deliver consistent parameter estimation. We employ folded concave penalties (FCP), including the well-known SCAD and MCP, to address this issue. Using FCP, we establish two asymptotic results: (i) a local oracle property for the penalized regression, and (ii) a global oracle property for regressions with a penalty-level constraint. In particular, the latter guarantees a global solution that consistently estimates the true coefficients and enjoys oracle prediction performance. Simulation studies and an application to predicting the euro area unemployment rate show that FCP improves variable selection and out-of-sample prediction relative to LASSO.

items.title: Robust Capital Budgeting
items.summary: We study capital budgeting when a manager privately knows project productivity and her empire-building benefits, while headquarters lacks credible priors. Headquarters minimizes maximum regret relative to informed investment. Without compensation, the optimal policy is a spending cap balancing empire-building overinvestment against profitable investment forgone. Compensation helps when empire-building incentives are weak. The optimal payment incentivizes restraint, declines with investment, and reaches zero at the spending cap, supporting greater managerial discretion. When empire-building incentives are strong, compensation cannot distinguish productive investment from biased expansion; therefore, a spending cap alone is optimal.

items.title: A Balanced Parametrization of Correlation Matrices
items.summary: We introduce the balanced correlation parametrization (BCP), which maps positive-definite correlation matrices one-to-one onto the set of symmetric hollow matrices. A key feature of the parametrization is that both the transformation and its inverse are available in closed form. It combines marginal and partial correlations, is inverse-consistent and equivariant under variable permutations and sign changes, and preserves block structure. A novel property of BCP is that it preserves correlation sparsity as the dimension tends to infinity under suitable factor conditions, providing a basis for sparse high-dimensional correlation modeling. An empirical illustration using standardized idiosyncratic daily stock returns for 1,765 equities over 15 years shows that BCP retains the approximate sparsity pattern and magnitudes of shock correlations, and that it yields accurate positive-definite reconstructions under sparse coordinate restrictions.

items.title: Representation Multiplicity in Causal Forests
items.summary: Including covariates alongside strictly monotone transformations can change a causal forest's treatment decisions without adding information. Random feature selection favors covariates represented by these multiple columns. Under stated conditions, I show that this imbalance can persist as samples grow. Treatment effect components associated with other covariates are omitted, attenuated, or recovered depending on their inclusion probabilities and tree depth. Simulations and a job-training replication illustrate sensitivity to redundant transformations. Sampling groups of variables that generate identical splits restores prediction invariance on the grouping data when fitting and randomization are held fixed.

items.title: Contracting for Decision-Relevant Beliefs
items.summary: An expert may misreport her forecast to influence a decision she cares about. We study contracts that elicit both her belief about a verifiable state and her stake in a binary action. If every belief is possible at two distinct stakes, exact incentive compatibility prevents a belief-only mechanism from letting the action depend on the report. Asking about both belief and stake allows the action to respond, but may require implementation rent. For threshold rules, we show that minimum rent equals the cutoff's positive curvature weighted by the belief distribution. The principal therefore chooses a cutoff by balancing virtual surplus against the implementation rent of truthful reporting. We characterize the best cutoff rule and give sufficient conditions under which it is optimal even among randomized mechanisms.

items.title: Designing Persuasive Experiments
items.summary: Incentives in experimental design are often misaligned: experimenters design and finance experiments to seek regulatory approval, while regulators seek to maximize social welfare. This incentive misalignment is especially relevant for Bayesian and adaptive trial designs, which have gained substantial popularity in recent years and have been actively encouraged by the US Food and Drug Administration. We propose a framework to resolve this conflict, wherein regulators set a minimum welfare threshold, and experimenters optimize designs subject to this constraint. It requires no knowledge of experimenters' private preferences or costs and mitigates strategic Bayesian persuasion. By varying the welfare threshold, we can map the Pareto frontier between the experimenter's and regulator's welfare. Under normal priors, Neyman allocation is always the optimal sampling strategy, regardless of specific objectives. We also characterize the optimal stopping rule. A numerical study calibrated to clinical trial data shows sample size reductions of over 48% relative to classical designs attaining the same social welfare.

items.title: Optimal Dynamic Majority-Quorum Rules: Theory and Evidence
items.summary: We study the optimal sequential aggregation of randomly arriving votes from a finite population to identify an unknown majority preference before a fixed deadline, trading off decision accuracy against the cost of delay. The optimal policy is a dynamic majority-quorum rule: a joint, time-varying threshold on vote lead and count, in which quorum and supermajority requirements emerge as the solution to an inference problem about non-participants' preferences. At each date, the continuation region is lens-shaped: the lead required to stop grows with turnout until too few voters remain to overturn it, and it vanishes at the deadline. We characterize conditions under which the boundary is monotone in the stakes, the arrival process, and time. Because the exact boundary admits no closed form, we derive a large-population approximation that reduces the two-dimensional rule onto a single sufficient statistic, and express the rule as a sequential significance test set by a single error tolerance. Calibrated on Polkadot governance data, an out-of-sample evaluation finds that our rule with a 2\% error tolerance halves decision times relative to the incumbent mechanism.

items.title: Conditional Disclosure as a Coordination Device
items.summary: People with controversial views may stay silent rather than speak out alone, though in a large enough group they could speak safely together. A Social Assurance Contract makes disclosure conditional: signed commitments of support stay private until enough people have signed for it to be safe to publish. In contrast, a survey can measure hidden support but does not make identification conditional on enough others joining. I derive the contract's exact advantage over speaking openly, and when that advantage disappears. Such contracts can turn a few people who would speak alone into a larger coalition.

items.title: Pregnancy and Interrupted Schooling: Evidence from Monthly Histories
items.summary: Pregnancy can disrupt schooling before infant care begins. We use monthly histories from the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth 1997 to study school interruptions during pregnancy and after childbirth and whether students later return to school or earn a diploma or GED. We jointly model conception and sustained interruptions in enrollment, allowing persistent unobserved differences to affect both processes. Under the timing-of-events identifying assumptions, pregnancy raises the monthly interruption rate to nearly four times the rate without pregnancy. Interruption rates are elevated before delivery and remain elevated afterward. After an interruption, students already exposed to pregnancy return to school and earn a diploma or GED less often within two years. These findings show that schooling disruption is already present during pregnancy, before the additional demands of infant care begin.

items.title: Safety Research and the Allocation of Frontier Compute
items.summary: Who should give up compute for AI safety research: customers or capability research? Safety paid for by customers delays no capability. Safety paid for by research slows the frontier, which gives knowledge more time to accumulate but postpones what a finished frontier provides. In a frontier-takeoff model, the cheaper source at a given allocation is set by a threshold in demand capacity. Demand capacity is the share of compute customers can use once the frontier is finished. Research should pay too only when demand capacity lies below the threshold. Where the threshold sits depends on how fast the value of customer services diminishes. In the calibration it rises with the service budget, because each further unit taken from customers costs them more. Safety paid for by customers should come early: its ratio to customer compute falls over the takeoff unless safety productivity rises fast. In a calibration with a tight service budget, early customer-funded safety lowers the probability of catastrophe from 75 to 51 percent. That is within one point of the best rule found that may also slow research.

items.title: Playing Against the Machine: Cooperation, Communication, and Strategy Heterogeneity in Repeated Prisoner's Dilemma
items.summary: This paper investigates how natural language communication with an AI agent affects human cooperative behaviour in indefinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma games. We conduct a laboratory experiment (n = 126) with two between-subjects treatments varying whether human participants chat with an AI chatbot (GPT-5.2) before every round or only before the first round of each supergame, and benchmark against human-human data from Dvorak and Fehrler (2024) (n = 108). We find four main results. First, cooperation against the AI is high and initially comparable to human-human levels, but unlike in the human-human setting, where cooperation converges to near-complete levels, cooperation against the AI plateaus and never reaches full cooperation. Second, repeated communication, which substantially increases cooperation in human-human interactions, has no detectable effect in the human-AI setting. Third, strategy estimation reveals that human-AI subjects favour Grim Trigger under pre-play communication and remain dispersed under repeated communication, whereas human-human subjects converge to Tit-for-Tat and unconditional cooperation respectively. Fourth, human-AI conversations contain more explicit strategy commitments but fewer emotional and social messages. These results suggest that humans cooperate with AI at high rates but do not develop the trust observed in human-human interactions. Cooperation in the human-AI setting is sustained through conditional rules rather than through the social bonds and mutual understanding that characterise human-human cooperation.

items.title: Designing Markets for Screening: Optimal Composition and the Geometry of Surplus
items.summary: We characterize the structure of market compositions that generate Pareto efficient outcomes and the geometry of the surplus set in a screening model with type-dependent costs. Maximizing principal or total surplus concentrates the market at the highest type, with all surplus extracted. Agent-oriented optima instead use, rather than suppress, screening: all agents in the market are served, there is no bunching, and a positive share of agents have the highest type and are served efficiently. Separation is valuable even under agent surplus maximization because it propagates information rents. Under a mild cost-curvature condition, each Pareto efficient outcome is implemented by a unique market. Under a stronger cost-curvature condition, the surplus set is convex whenever values are private, or types with no gains from trade can be included in the market. We characterize all surplus outcomes in these cases. Without such types and with type-dependent costs, the surplus set can be nonconvex. Market segmentation generates the missing outcomes but does not increase the maximum agent surplus at any level of principal surplus. We also derive comparative statics along the Pareto frontier and with respect to value-cost co-movement, distinguishing changes in market composition from changes in individual allocations and rents.

items.title: Shaping the Menu: Information Design under Screening
items.summary: How should consumers learn when a seller chooses a menu of product qualities and prices? We study information design when the seller observes the learning policy, but not consumers' private signals, before choosing its menu. Under cost-curvature conditions, we characterize optimal learning when consumer surplus receives greater weight than profit. Even with two valuations, every optimal posterior distribution combines an interval of posterior types with an efficiently served atom at the highest valuation. The induced menu features a continuum of differentiated products. Strikingly, optimal learning can also induce a lower posterior atom, separated from this interval by a support gap. Buyers in this atom either purchase an isolated low-quality product or are excluded, even when trade with every buyer creates gains. Both configurations can be optimal for the same prior and welfare weight. Served buyers with distinct posterior types are never bunched at the same quality. General finite priors can yield several separating regions and trading atoms. We also characterize the optimal joint design of learning and valuation-dependent segmentation, showing, among other results, that every posterior type with positive gains from trade must be served. Joint design can raise both consumer surplus and profit relative to buyer-optimal private learning alone. Even random assignment to segments with different learning policies and separate menus can give consumers more surplus than any single market yielding the same profit. Additional price discrimination can therefore benefit consumers, even when privacy restrictions require segmentation to reveal nothing about valuations to the seller.

items.title: Truthful Production Uncertainty in Electricity Markets: A Two-Stage Mechanism
items.summary: Renewable power sources have low production costs, but may result in high balancing costs due to the inherent production uncertainty. Current day-ahead markets elicit only point production profiles and neglect the degree of uncertainty associated with each generating asset, preventing the market operator from accounting for balancing costs in day-ahead dispatch and ancillary service procurement. This increases the total system cost and undermines market efficiency, especially in renewable-heavy power systems. To address this, we propose a new market clearing paradigm based on a two-stage mechanism, where producers report their production forecast distribution in the day-ahead stage, followed by the realized production in the real-time stage. By extending the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) payments to the two-stage setting, we show appealing properties in terms of incentive compatibility and individual rationality. An electricity market case study validates the theoretical claims, illustrating the effectiveness of the proposed mechanism in reducing system cost.

items.title: The Robustness of Sequential Implementation under Information Perturbations
items.summary: Bayesian monotonicity is a necessary condition for full implementation in Bayes-Nash equilibrium. Under the sequential equilibrium refinement, however, multi-stage mechanisms can expand the scope for implementation. We show that this additional implementation power is fragile. Whenever a multi-stage mechanism sequentially implements a social choice correspondence that is not Bayesian monotone, we construct arbitrarily small "information perturbations" and show that there are sequential equilibria under these perturbations that yield inadmissible decisions with probability bounded away from zero. Under these perturbations, players' types are not independent conditional on the state and some player is sometimes uncertain of their payoff type. We show by example that the general result fails if perturbations are required to satisfy conditional independence or "known payoff types."

items.title: Higher-Order Neyman Orthogonality in Moment-Condition Models
items.summary: We construct moment functions that are Neyman-orthogonal to a chosen order in parametric moment condition models involving nuisance parameters. These moment functions reduce sensitivity to estimation error in the nuisance parameters and, as such, offer a unified and tractable route to higher-order debiasing in a wide range of econometric models.
